utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 4th of May, 2011. Let me first greet the prominent OTP representatives who attend the hearing for the oral decision by the Trial Chamber under Rule 98 bis. Let me also greet Mr. Seselj and all the people assisting us, the Registrar, the usher, the security officer, and any other people assisting us. Today I shall start with the reading out of the Rule 98 bis decision, and then I will continue with a partially dissenting opinion of mine. We are to sit in the morning today. We're going to start right now, and we shall more likely than not continue into the afternoon. If I were not to be finished with reading out the decision, we can continue tomorrow afternoon, because I have over 120 pages to read. I shall start. The Trial Chamber is going to deliver its Rule 98 bis decision, oral decision. Firstly, the Trial Chamber will recall the procedural background and then will move on to the law applicable under Rule 98 bis. Thirdly, it will recall the counts and modes of responsibility as alleged in the indictment. Fourthly, it will recall the elements of the crimes and set out the law applicable to instigating as a mode of participation in crimes. In a fifth part, it will give samples of evidence it has heard that are enough and capable of supporting at this stage of the proceedings to sustain the allegations as alleged in the counts, and then the Trial Chamber will review the responsibility of the accused for instigating to crimes as alleged in the indictment through his speeches. First, procedural background. The Prosecution case started on the 7th of November, 2009 and closed with the testimony of Witness Nenad Jovic on the 7th of July, 2010. Further on, the Prosecution would not rest its case until the Trial Chamber had ruled on all of their pending motions, including various applications for the testimony of witnesses, including VS-026, considered as being unavailable for health reasons following a first expert medical report. The Trial Chamber decided to have VS-026 examined by a medical expert and his opinion confirms the first, in a report filed on the 26th of November, 2010. The Trial Chamber then ruled all of the pending motions in December 2010, on all the motions that might have an impact on the Rule 98 bis proceedings by handing down 25 decisions. The Trial Chamber then had to wait for the filing of the expert report as to the authenticity of the Mladic notebooks filed on the 10th of January, 2010, its translation into B/C/S and the end of the time limit for the accused to make submissions, if any, as to the motion to admit the notebooks. At the administrative hearing of the 18th of January, 2011, the accused informed the Trial Chamber that it would -- he would make submissions under Rule 98 bis. The Trial Chamber, taking into account the time needed to rule on the motions for review of the decisions issued in December filed by the Prosecution between the 28th of December and the 21st of January, 2011, issued a Scheduling Order on the 25th of January for the Rule 98 bis proceedings to be held on the 7th, 8th, and 9th of March, 2011. On the 7th of March, 2011, the accused made his oral submissions under Rule 98 bis. He spoke again on the 9th of March in order to reply to the Prosecution specifically. The accused denied having committed, ordered, planned, aided and abetted or instigated any of the crimes alleged in the indictment. He also challenges and denies having participated in the crimes as a member of a joint criminal enterprise. More specifically, the accused challenged the existence of specific crimes as alleged in the indictment under various counts, as well as their credibility of numerous testimony and other Prosecution evidence. Furthermore, he claims that the Prosecution failed to lead any evidence as to the speeches in Vukovar, Mali Zvornik, and Hrtkovci as alleged in the indictment, inasmuch as he did not give such speeches. He further argues that if certain crimes may have been committed, there is no evidence that the crimes should be attributed to the volunteers recruited by his party, the Serbian Radical Party, hereinafter known as SRS. He states that he can by no means be held responsible for crimes allegedly committed by such volunteers since the accused was not their superior within the JNA in which their volunteers were serving. In conclusion, the accused stressed that it was impossible to prove beyond any reasonable doubt that criminal acts can be attributed to him, and he is of the view that the Trial Chamber shall therefore have to enter a judgement of acquittal on all counts in the indictment. The Prosecution responded to the accused's submissions at the hearings of the 8th and 9th of March, 2011. It drew the attention of the Chamber on various testimony and evidence admitted by the Trial Chamber which is such that they would not be capable of sustaining a decision of acquittal. Law applicable further to Rule 98 bis. Under Rule 98 bis, once the Prosecution case is closed, the Trial Chamber must, by oral decision and after hearing oral submissions by the parties, enter a decision of acquittal as to any count for which there is no evidence capable of sustaining a conviction. Since the 8th of December, 2004, when Rule 98 bis was last amended. A Trial Chamber is only expected to determine whether the Prosecution has adduced enough evidence for each count taken as a whole as opposed to all the various charges making up that particular count. Rule 98 bis was amended in order to facilitate the proceedings and to provide for a more expeditious trial. First of all, because it moved from written to an oral type of proceedings, and also on focusing on all of the counts rather than on every single crime alleged in each and every count of the indictment. Therefore, since the latest amendment of Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber in its majority, Judge Antonetti dissenting, deems that it can only enter a decision of acquittal on a single count as a whole, and this is, by the way, in keeping with the practice applied after Rule 98 bis was amended. It was adopted and applied by Trial Chambers in the following cases, among others: Martic, Mrksic, Prlic and Gotovina. The fact that the Trial Chamber is under the obligation to enter a decision of acquittal on the whole count gives the Defence the possibility not to answer to all of the allegations contained in a count for which it feels that the Prosecution failed to lead any evidence. Under Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber needs to determine whether there is enough evidence for a reasonable trier of fact to enter a judgement of conviction beyond any reasonable doubt. At this stage, the Trial Chamber is not to establish whether it would enter a conviction at the end of the trial proceedings but whether it could do so. It should be stressed that at the Rule 98 bis stage of the proceedings, according to the Rules, the Trial Chamber will first carry out a preliminary examination of the evidence adduced in the Prosecution case in order to ascertain whether the evidence is capable of sustaining a conviction. This is a preliminary examination which is different from the analysis carried out at the end of the trial proceedings. Indeed, at the end of the trial, a Trial Chamber must look in depth into the entire case file to examine every evidence on record, be it Prosecution or Defence evidence in order to assess their respective probative value. In order to carry out this first assessment at this stage of the proceedings under Rule 98 bis, the Trial Chamber must factor in all the evidence adduced during the Prosecution case. It is not to make a selection among the Prosecution evidence. The evidence favourable to the accused may only be used to assess whether a piece of evidence is clearly unreliable and incapable of belief. As a consequence, a motion for acquittal will be granted only when there is no evidence capable of sustaining a conviction or when there is one or several pieces of evidence, but even when taken at its highest, this evidence the Trial Chamber could not sustain or decide for a conviction because the only evidence is clearly unreliable and incapable of belief. The Trial Chamber further recalls that it will only give some examples of evidence. The fact that specific evidence has -- have been taken into account for the purposes of this instant decision does not mean that the Trial Chamber will assess them in the same way at the final stage of the judgement. Equally, the fact that specific evidence may not be mentioned in this decision does not mean that it will not be taken into account and assessed accordingly at the end of the judgement, in the judgement stage. Furthermore, whilst the accused is charged under various modes of responsibilities, it is sufficient for the majority of the Trial Chamber Judges, Judge Antonetti, myself, dissenting, it is sufficient to establish that there is evidence supporting one single mode of responsibility alleged in the indictment to dismiss a motion for acquittal. Therefore, if a Trial Chamber accepts one of the modes of responsibility at this stage of the proceeding does not mean that the Trial Chamber ruled out the other modes of responsibilities -- responsibility alleged in the indictment. Thus a Trial Chamber may, when it issues its final judgement choose another mode of responsibility that was mentioned at the Rule 98 bis proceedings. The Trial Chamber further stresses that it is for the Trial Chamber to assess the type of responsibility to attribute to the accused on the basis of the indictment and on the basis of the trial record as has already been affirmed and confirmed by the Tribunal in paragraph 248 of the Kvocka judgement. Finally, the Trial Chamber wants to make it clear that there is no contradiction between the dismissal of a Rule 98 bis motion and a decision of acquittal at the end of the trial proceedings. This applies even if the Defence has not adduced any evidence. Third section, overview of the counts and modes of responsibility as alleged in the indictment. Before I continue, I think I should slow down so that the interpreters can keep pace with me and do their job properly. I'm looking at the English transcript on the screen, and I'm listening to the B/C/S booth. So far, so good. Third section, overview of the counts and modes of responsibility as alleged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber recalls that in the third amended indictment filed on the 7th of December, 2007, herein before and hereinafter known as the indictment, the Prosecution charges the accused with crimes referred to in the Statute of the Tribunal, namely crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war. The charges alleged in the indictment against the accused include the following nine counts: Count 1, persecution on political, racial, or religious grounds, a crime against humanity. Count 4, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war. Count 8, torture, a violation of the laws or customs of war. Count 9, cruel treatment, a violation of the laws or customs of war. Count 10, deportation, a crime against humanity. Count 11, forcible transfer, inhumane act, a crime against humanity. Count 12, wanton destruction of villages or devastation not justified by military necessity, a violation of the laws or customs of war. Count 13, destruction or wilful damage to institutions dedicated to religion or education, a violation of the laws or customs of war. Counted 14, plunder of public or private property, a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber will examine these counts in two groups as to whether they are alleged as crimes against humanity or as war crimes. The crimes the accused is charged with in the indictment concern the municipalities of Vukovar in Croatia, Zvornik, Sarajevo, Mostar, Nevesinje in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Hrtkovci in Vojvodina in Serbia. The accused is charged on the basis of his individual criminal responsibility under all the forms of responsibility referred to in Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. For all the crimes alleged in the indictment, under paragraph 5 of the indictment, it reads as follows -- I'm going to read out paragraph 5 of the indictment, which is a major one: "Vojislav Seselj is individually criminally responsible for the crimes referred to in Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal and described in this indictment, which he planned, ordered, instigated, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution thereof. "By using the word 'committed,' the Prosecution does not intend to suggest that the accused physically committed all of the crimes charged personally. Physical commitment is pleaded only in relation to the charges of persecutions by direct and public ethnic denigration with respect to the accused's speeches in Vukovar, Mali Zvornik, and Hrtkovci, and by deportation and forcible transfer with respect to his speech in Hrtkovci and in relation to the charges of deportation and inhumane acts, forcible transfer with respect to his speech in Hrtkovci. "In this indictment, 'committed' includes the participation of Vojislav Seselj as a co-perpetrator in a joint criminal enterprise. By using the word 'instigated,' the Prosecution charges that the speeches, communications, acts and/or omissions of Vojislav Seselj contributed to the perpetrators' decision to commit the crimes alleged." So this was the entire paragraph 5 of the indictment. The Trial Chamber recalls that if the accused denied any responsibility under any mode of responsibility as alleged in the indictment, this decision will endeavour for the sake of judicial economy to review the evidence related to the alleged responsibility of the accused solely as regards instigation. Indeed, as we already recalled, in the view of the Trial Chamber's majority, because I have a dissenting opinion, it is enough for the purposes of the Rule 98 bis proceedings to establish that there is evidence capable of sustaining one single form of responsibility alleged in the indictment to dismiss a motion for acquittal. This does not mean, however, that the Trial Chamber may not later on rule as to the other modes of responsibility. Fourth section, overview of the elements of crimes and the law applicable to instigation as a mode of liability. With regard to the elements of crimes, first, the Trial Chamber recalls that according to Articles 2, 4, and 5 of the Statute, crimes of war, as well as crimes against humanity occur in the context of a domestic or international armed conflict. Secondly, the Trial Chamber recalls that to constitute a crime against humanity, the actions of an accused must be part of a generalised or systematic attack directed against a civilian population -- any civilian population. These two qualifiers are alternative and not cumulative. The qualifier "generalisee" means that the attack was carried out in a very large scale and resulted in a great number of victims, whereas the qualifier "systematic" shows the organised nature of these violent acts and the fact that their randomness is improbable. The systematic nature is recognised through the deliberate and regular repetition of similar criminal behaviours. Thirdly, regarding the actus reus of the crimes, it will be reviewed later by the Trial Chamber when the Trial Chamber addresses the counts alleged in the indictment. Fourthly, the Trial Chamber recalls that the mens rea for each crime alleged in all nine counts is made up of the criminal intent of the perpetrator of the crime, except for the crime of persecution, where in addition, in order for the responsibility of an accused to be engaged, there is need for a dolus specialis, i.e., a specific intent to discriminate on political, racial, or religious grounds. The Trial Chamber will revisit this later on when it analyses count number 1. Section B, regarding the law applicable to instigation as a mode of liability. For a Trial Chamber to conclude that there has been instigation to commit crimes it must make sure that three conditions are met. First, a condition relating to the elements of instigation; secondly, a condition relating to the intent of the instigator; and thirdly, a condition relating to the nexus between the instigation and the crime. First, regarding the elements of instigation to the commission of crimes. The case law of this Tribunal, notably paragraph 27 of the Kordic and Cerkez appeal judgement, defined "instigation" as, I quote: "Provoking someone into committing an offence." The case law of the ICTR, notably in paragraph 456 of the Ndindabahizi judgement defined instigation as "pushing," I quote, "pushing or encouraging someone else, either verbally or through any other means of communication to commit a crime with the intent of this crime to be committed." Therefore, as mentioned in paragraph 271 of the Oric judgement, in order to have an actus reus that would make up instigation, the instigator must have influenced the physical perpetrator of the crime by requesting him to do so, by pushing him to do so, or by making sure by some way that he would actually commit the crime. However, this did not presuppose necessarily that the instigator would have originated the idea, would have designed the initial plan in order to commit the crime. Even if the main perpetrator already envisaged the commission of the crime, the fact that he actually carried out his intent might come from having been persuaded or asked to do so by the instigator. More specifically regarding how the main perpetrator was influenced, there is no need for the instigation to commit crimes referred to by the Statute be public or direct as it is the case for the direct and public instigation to commit genocide, which is a crime in itself and not a mode of liability. As indicated in paragraph 273 of the Oric judgement, the influence coming from instigation can be exerted directly or through intermediaries, and this on various amount of people as long as the instigator has the required mens rea. There is no need for the instigator to be on the scene of crime as stated by the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR in paragraph 660 of the Nahimana appeals judgement, which is more known as the Media appeals judgement. Secondly, regarding the mens rea of the instigator. The Trial Chamber must demonstrate that the -- it is important to demonstrate that the accused had the intent to provoke or to induce the perpetration of a crime or that he was well aware that there was a real probability that, after his instigation, one or more crimes would be committed, in the single or in the plural. In this respect, the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 32 of the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement indicated that anyone provoking another person into committing an act or an omission while being aware that there is a real probability that a crime could be committed during the execution of this -- of this instigation has the required mens rea to be held responsible under Article 7(1) of the Statute. The fact of instigating while being fully aware of this probability must be considered as accepting the crime that will result. The Trial Chamber, however, notes that for the crimes alleged in counts 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14 as charged in the indictment, it will be sufficient to prove that the accused was fully aware that there was a real probability that after the instigation one of these crimes would be committed. However, regarding the crime alleged in count 1, there is need also to verify whether the accused had the intention to provoke or to induce the commission of persecution as a crime aimed at achieving the specific goal of discriminating on political, racial, or religious grounds. Finally, the Trial Chamber notes that there must -- that a difference must be made between the intent and the personal motivation. As stated by the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 102 of the Krnojelac appeals judgement, the existence of a personal motivation does not prevent the perpetrator of a crime from being -- from having the necessary mens rea. Thirdly, regarding the existence of a nexus between instigation and commission of the crime. As stated by the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 27 of the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement, there is no need to prove that the crime would not have been committed without the involvement of the accused. It is sufficient to show that instigation was a significant element in the behaviour of the physical perpetrator of the crimes. Similarly, in paragraph 660 of the Media appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR specified that in order to have instigation to commit a crime, it is important to establish that the actions charged substantially contributed to the crime being committed. However, it is not necessary for these actions to have been a sine qua non condition of the commission of the said crime. Furthermore, the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR, in paragraph 257 of the Semanza appeals judgement specified that it was not necessary to show or demonstrate that the accused had an effective control over the perpetrator of the crime. In paragraphs 238 and 296 of this appeals judgement, the Appeals Chamber stated that neither was it necessary for the indictment to state the exact provocative words spoken by the accused or to provide any evidence of it to establish instigation to commit crimes. Finally, in paragraph 368 of the Nchamihigo judgement, the ICTR indicated that the time period between instigation and commission of a crime is also a relevant criteria to determine the substantial contribution to instigation of commission of a crime. As a consequence, the nexus between the elements of instigation on the one hand and the crimes alleged in the indictment on the other hand can be inferred from a number of indicia taking into consideration elements such as, for example, the position of authority and the influence exerted by the accused over the physical perpetrators of the alleged crimes or the time period between the instigation and the commission of the crimes, or the crime. Section number 5. The Trial Chamber in its majority, dissenting opinion from Judge Antonetti, will now state why any reasonable trier of fact could conclude beyond any reasonable doubt that in this case, at this stage of the proceedings, there is sufficient evidence to support the commission of crimes as alleged in all nine counts. First, the Trial Chamber underscores that the accused did not contest the fact that there was an armed conflict at the time as far as the crimes alleged in the nine counts are -- are concerned. The Trial Chamber also notes that the accused even stated about the war in Bosnia that it was both a religious and a civil war. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber notes that the evidence on the trial record almost all state that there was an armed conflict going on, as far as crimes against humanity are concerned as well as crimes of war. (a), regarding crimes against humanity under counts 1, 10, and 11. First and foremost, the Trial Chamber would like to answer the submissions of the accused who contests -- who challenges the fact that the crimes alleged in the indictment under counts 1, 10, and 11 would have been committed in the framework of a generalised or systematic attack. The Trial Chamber considers that at this stage of the proceedings, it has a large amount of evidence which will be mentioned more specifically later. This evidence would allow any reasonable trier of fact to conclude beyond any reasonable doubt that the crimes alleged under count 1, relating to persecution as a crime against humanity and under counts 10 and 11 relating to deportation and forcible transfer as crimes against humanity were part of a generalised attack against non-Serb civilian population with the goal of expelling them from the territories of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; from the municipalities of Zvornik; from the region of Sarajevo; from Mostar; Nevesinje; and from some parts of Vojvodina in Serbia. Therefore, there is no need for the Trial Chamber to examine at this stage of the proceedings to -- to the question of knowing whether these facts were committed in the framework of a systematic attack. Secondly, the Trial Chamber will now give examples of evidence that could support the fact that each crimes alleged in counts 1, 10, and 11 of the indictment were committed and that the attack against the non-Serb civilian population had a -- was of a generalised nature. Number one, as far as count 1 is concerned, i.e., persecution as a crime against humanity the Trial Chamber would like to recall first as stated in paragraph 985 of the Media appeals judgement that the crime of persecution is an act or an omission which introduces a de facto discrimination and which refutes or violates a fundamental right recognised by the international customary law or by the conventional law and which has been deliberately committed with the intent to discriminate for an unlawful motivation, notably to discriminate on racial, religious, or political grounds. However, any act of discrimination does not equate to a crime of persecution. The acts underlying persecution making up a crime against humanity, be it -- be they in isolation or jointly with other acts must present the same degree of seriousness than the crimes listed under Article 5 of the Statute. Furthermore, even though persecution often implies a series of actions, a single action may be enough as long as the act or the omission is discriminatory in facts and was deliberately perpetrated with the intent of discriminating for an unlawful reason. Therefore, as stated by the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement, murder, mistreatment, unlawful attacks against civilian property or individuals, the illegal detention of civilians, the destruction of civilian property and plunder are elements of persecutions similar to -- which can be equated to a crime against humanity when they are -- either when they're taken in isolation or jointly with other actions. To establish that there have been persecutions as elements of a crime against humanity, it is necessary, in addition, to prove that the perpetrator of the underlying actus reus had a specific intent to discriminate for unlawful reasons, notably on political, racial, or religious grounds. The required discriminatory intent cannot be directly inferred from the generally -- from the general discriminatory nature of an attack qualified as a crime against humanity. However, the Appeals Chamber, in paragraph 110 of the Kordic and Cerkez appeals judgement, considers, and I quote: "The discriminatory intent can be inferred from such a context subject to the existence, as far as the facts are concerned, circumstances surrounding the commission of the crimes alleged which confirm the existence of such an intent." In this case, the persecution alleged in the indictment aimed to expel non-Serb population from a number of regions, i.e., Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, from the municipalities of Zvornik, of the region of Sarajevo, of Mostar, of Nevesinje, and of certain areas of Vojvodina in Serbia. The Trial Chamber also notes that the elements underlying persecution as referred to in the indictment mainly correspond, as far as time and -- in -- as far as time is concerned and location is concerned too, the crimes alleged under the other counts, i.e., deportation and forcible transfer as crimes against humanity, as well as murder, torture, inhuman -- cruel treatment, destruction, and plunder of property protected by the Geneva Conventions as crimes of war. There are also -- there are also other underlying acts of persecution as alleged in the indictment. There are other acts such as the application of restrictive measures and discriminatory measures towards non-Serb civilians, and public and direct denigration in speeches made in Vukovar, Mali Zvornik, and Hrtkovci, promoting hatred of Croats, Muslims, and other non-Serb populations. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused denies all allegations under count 1 relating to persecutions. The accused notably challenges the allegations of religious discrimination and states that he never gave any speech in Mali Zvornik in 1992, that no speech was delivered during the war in Vukovar, and that during his speech in Hrtkovci in the framework of his electoral campaign, he only supported the idea of an exchange of civilian population and the principle of retorsion. Therefore, the accused submits that the Croats left in the framework of voluntary exchanges of property and not in the framework of a campaign of persecution aimed at expelling them. The accused also specifies that in the assumption that the deportation and forcible transfer would have been recognised, these crimes did not -- would not reach the necessary intensity to be sanctioned as persecution as referred under Article 5 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber cannot take into consideration this last submission, which is totally unsustainable. Apart from the fact that as far as the generalised nature of the persecution of non-Serb population, the Prosecution had a large amount of elements. The seriousness, notably of the deportation and forcible transfer, also results obviously from the provisions of the Geneva Convention of 1949. Article 49 of the Fourth Convention bans forcible transfers, be it en masse or individual, as well as expulsion of protected people outside the occupied territory to send them towards a territory of the occupying power or toward -- to the -- to the territory of any other state, be it an occupied state or not and for whatever reason. This provision is mentioned again in Article 85 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions for international armed conflicts and in Article 17 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions in case of domestic armed conflict. The Trial Chamber specifies moreover that in the Statute, the term "deportation" in English has been translated as "expulsion" in French, and that this crime is presently provided for as a crime that can constitute a crime against humanity under Article 5, in paragraph (D) of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber in the appeals judgement Krnojelac held that the crime of persecution may take on different forms. It may be one of the other acts that make up the elements of the crimes charged in Article 5 of the Statute or one of the acts that make up the elements of crimes in other Articles of the Statute. One can therefore not challenge the fact that expulsions and forcible transfers may constitute underlying acts of the crime of persecution when they are committed individually or accumulatively with the requisite discriminatory intent. As regards actus reus of the underlying crimes of persecution alleged in the indictment, the Trial Chamber will analyse the -- these hereinafter pertaining to the commission of crimes charged under counts 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13. Therefore, the Chamber shall now address, and only address as an example, some of the evidence it has on the commission of persecution that would allow a reasonable judge to support at this stage of the 98 bis decision the fact that the perpetrators of the underlying material acts had the requisite discriminatory intent. Before I continue, I would like to mention that I'm going to quote names of witnesses and exhibit numbers. Since there are many of them, there might be some names of the witnesses that are misspelt and some figures may be recorded incorrectly. This will be corrected at a later stage. The Registry will have the document I'm reading from and will check that the names and the exhibit numbers are correct. So if there are any mistakes, don't worry about it. These mistakes will be corrected. I shall endeavour to read this out slowly. As regards the existence of a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population in the municipality of Zvornik, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses Fadil Banjanovic, VS-1064, and VS-1066 that testified to those facts on the basis of which the Chamber may infer that the specific criminal intent existed. As regards evidence on the imposition of restrictive and discriminatory measures against non-Serb civilians including restrictions of movement, removal from positions of authority in local government institutions and the police, dismissal from jobs, denial of medical care and arbitrary searches of homes in the municipality of Mostar, the Chamber refers, as an example, to witnesses VS-1068, VS-1067, and to Exhibits P658 under seal, P659 under seal, P1052 under seal, who testified to these facts, and on the basis of which the Chamber may infer that the specific criminal intent existed. As regards the municipality of Nevesinje, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses Ibrahim Kujan and Vojislav Dabic and to Exhibits P524 and P880 under seal that testify to facts of the same nature and on the basis of which the Chamber may infer that the specific criminal intent existed. As regards the area of Sarajevo, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses VS-1055 and VS-1111 and Exhibit P456 under seal that testify to facts of the same nature and on the basis of which the Chamber may infer that the specific criminal intent existed -- specific requisite criminal intent existed. As regards the Vojvodina, the Chamber refers to witnesses Aleksa Ejic and Katica Paulic who testify to facts of the same nature and on the basis of which the Chamber may infer that the specific requisite criminal intent existed. Now, as regards counts 10 and 11, on expulsion of non-Serb civilians as a crime against humanity and on the forcible transfer of this population as an inhumane act and a crime against humanity, the Trial Chamber notes that the accused argues that in Hrtkovci, inter alia, but also in other municipality, the departure of the non-Serb population occurred as part of an exchange of -- of property, allowing for the possibility of staying for those who so wished. The Trial Chamber remarks furthermore that the accused indicated on page 16694 of the transcript that at his speech in Hrtkovci he had promised that when the -- he would come to power, he would see to the exchange of property and would apply the principle of retorsion. I waited because the English interpreter was faster than the Serbian interpreter. On this point, it is important to recall that according to the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 229 of the Krnojelac appeals judgement, the Trial Chamber cannot infer that there is a real choice because consent was given insofar as the circumstances under which it was given may deprive it of any value. Accordingly, the evidence received by the Chamber that mentioned a consent must be reviewed in their context, bearing in mind the situation of insecurity and the climate of fear that prevailed, the threats and other forms of violence, the fear and the vulnerable position of the persons in question. Therefore, it is a lack of real choice, which is important in determining the unlawful nature of expulsion or forcible transfer. In the present trial, the Chamber considers that the fact that the accused tries to substantiate resorting to expulsion and forcible transfer of non-Serb civilians as relevant because this would amount to legal retorsion measures under international law. The Trial Chamber shall now provide a few examples of the evidence which is sufficient to base its analysis to consider that the crimes charged in counts 10 and 11 were in fact committed in the various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. As regards the municipality of Vukovar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the testimonies of the expert Anna-Maria Radic, of Dragutin Berghofer, and of Vesna Bosanac and to Exhibit numbers P278, P587 under seal, and P632. As regards the municipality of Zvornik, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the testimonies of Fadil Banjanovic, VS-1012, VS-1013, VS-1064, and to Exhibit numbers P663, P664, and P665. As far as the Sarajevo area is concerned, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the testimony of Safet Sejdic and to Exhibit number P463. As regards the municipality of Nevesinje, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the testimonies of Goran Stoparic and Ibrahim Kujan, as well as Exhibit number P524. As regards Vojvodina, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the testimonies of Aleksa Ejic, VS-1134, VS-061 and to Exhibit numbers P537 under seal and P564 under seal. As now -- as regards war crimes, now, alleged in counts 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, and 14. Firstly, as regards count 4, namely the murder of non-Serb civilians as a violation of the laws or customs of war. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused challenges the murder of some people in Velepromet, and he seems not to admit the existence of the alleged crimes committed in the municipality of Zvornik, save for the murder of 20 or so men and young Muslim boys and Croatians from Bosnia for whom the accused underscores this should be attributed solely to Arkan's men. The Chamber shall now provide a few examples of the evidence which is sufficient and which -- on which it can base its review to consider at this stage of the 98 bis procedure that the crime of murder charged under count 4 was, in fact, committed in the various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. As regards the municipality of Vukovar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the following evidence: As regards the execution of non-Serbs by the Serbian forces on an execution site located between the Ovcara farm and Grabovo, close to Vukovar, on the 20th of November, 1991, the Chamber heard the witnesses VS-016, VS-007, Emil Cakalic, as well as Davor Strinovic. The Chamber has also received the Exhibits P609, P611, P615, P782, and P786. Furthermore, as regards the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital and the execution of some of the prisoners at the Velepromet warehouse, the Chamber has heard the testimonies of Dragutin Berghofer and of VS-051 and has received Exhibit number P282. As regards the municipality of Zvornik, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the following evidence: On the murders committed at the Ekonomija Farm and at the Ciglana factory, the Chamber has heard the testimonies of witnesses VS-1015 and Fadil Kopic. Furthermore, as regards the murder of the Bosnian Muslims at the technical school of Karakaj, the Chamber has heard the testimony of VS-1012. As regards the murder of the detainees at the slaughterhouse of Gero, the Chamber heard the testimony of VS-1066. As regards the murder of Muslims committed at the cultural centre of Drinjaca, the Chamber heard witness VS-1064. As regards the area of Sarajevo, the Chamber refers, for instance to, the following evidence: As regards the execution of non-Serb civilians killed at Ljesevo in the municipality of Ilijas, the Chamber heard Witness VS-1111; on the murder of non-Serbs in Zuc in the municipality of Vogosca, the Chamber heard Witness Safet Sejdic. As regards the municipality of Mostar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the following evidence: On the murder of non-Serb civilians at the Vrapcici stadium, the Chamber heard Witness Redzep Karisik and has received Exhibit Number P481. As regards the execution of non-Serb civilians at the mortuary in Sutina, the Chamber heard Witness Fahrudin Bilic. Lastly regarding the municipality of Nevesinje, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the following evidence: On the murder of men whose bodies were found at Teleca Lastva, the Chamber has heard Witness VS-1022 and has received Exhibit Number P523. Now, as regards counts 8 and 9, namely torture and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war for which the Prosecution alleges detention and confinement under inhumane and brutal conditions of non-Serb civilians, including forcible labour and sexual assault and violence. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused challenges the allegations of -- of forced labour in the municipality of Vukovar. The accused admits furthermore the allegations of sexual violence in the municipality of Zvornik but holds that these incidents took place at the end of May until the beginning of June of 1992, according to the accused therefore before the volunteers of the SCP or the SRS were present in the area, which would mean that the accused could not be held responsible for these sexual assaults. The Chamber will now provide a few examples of some of the sufficient evidence it bases its review on to consider this stage of the 98 bis proceedings that the crimes charged in counts 8 and 9 were in fact committed in the various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. As regards the municipality of Vukovar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to the following evidence: As regards detention and confinement in brutal and inhumane conditions of non-Serb civilians at the Velepromet warehouse, the Chamber heard witnesses Dragutin Berghofer and VS-051. On detention and confinement under brutal and inhuman conditions of non-Serb civilians at the Ovcara farm, the Chamber heard witnesses Vojnovic and VS-016. I shall now make a break, because we need to have a break. I have read approximately half of the Trial Chamber's decision. We shall have a 30-minute break. I would like the Registrar to turn off the air-conditioning which is above my head, because I will be frozen solid before the end of the hearing otherwise, and I will be unable to speak. My voice will then be totally frozen. We shall now have a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Let me recall that I'm currently reading part of the oral decision which relates to the second paragraph, counts 8 and 9. I had stopped when I spoke about the municipality of Zvornik. Now, as regards the municipality of Zvornik, the Chamber refers, for instance, to testimonies of VS-1012, VS-1013, VS-1064, and VS-1065, and has received Exhibit numbers P307, P381 under seal, and P469 under seal. As far as the Sarajevo area is concerned, the Chamber refers, for instance, to Witness VS-1055 and has received Exhibits P455 and P457. As regards the municipality of Mostar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses Redzic Karisik and Fahrudin Bilic. Lastly, as regards the municipality of Nevesinje, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses VS-1022 and VS-1051. Section three, as regards the crimes charged in count number 12 -- in count 12, namely wanton destruction of villages and devastation not justified by military necessity as a violation of the laws or customs of war, the victims of which were non-Serbs. The Chamber notes that the accused does not mention anything about the commission of these crimes but rejects any involvement of the SCP/SRS volunteers in the said crimes. The Chamber will now provide some examples of the evidence it uses at this stage of the 98 bis proceedings to consider that the crimes charged in count 12 were, in fact, committed in the various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. As regards the municipality of Vukovar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses Dragutin Berghofer, Nebojsa Stojanovic, VS-021 and Exhibits P268, P278, and P526 under seal. As regards the area of Sarajevo, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses VS-1111, and VS-1055. As regards the municipality of Mostar, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witness 92 quater Zoran Tot and to Witness VS-1067, as well as Exhibits P843, P846, and P1051 under seal. Lastly, as regards the municipality of Nevesinje, the Chamber refers, for instance, to witnesses VS-1051, Ibrahim Kujan and Goran Stoparic as well as Exhibits P483 under seal and P524. With regard to the crimes alleged in count 13, namely destruction or wilful damage to institutions dedicated to education or religion of the non-Serb population as a violation of the laws or customs of war, the Trial Chamber notes that the accused's claim that these institution had been occupied for military purposes, were no longer protected by the Geneva Conventions. In this respect the Trial Chamber notes that during the 98 bis hearing, the accused failed to mention any document or evidence in support of his claim. The Trial Chamber also notes that there is evidence that there were cases of destruction whilst there was no armed formation around. The Trial Chamber, for instance, refers to the testimony of Witness VS-1055 as evidence of the fact. The Trial Chamber recalls that in any case, the protection or the protected status of a building dedicated to religion or education may not be lost simply because there are right next to it military activities or facilities. Indeed, it is the use made of the premises and not their location that determines whether the premises in question may lose their protected status as this was reaffirmed on many occasions by this Tribunal, for instance, in paragraph 310 of the Strugar judgement, in paragraph 604 of the Naletilic judgement, and in paragraph 98 of the Martic judgement. The Trial Chamber will now provide some examples of evidence it deemed sufficient at the 98 bis stage of the proceedings that crimes in count 13 were indeed committed in various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. Regarding the municipality of Zvornik. The Trial Chamber, for instance, heard expert Witness Andras Riedlmayer and witnesses Asim Alic, VS-037, and VS-038. Regarding Greater Sarajevo, the Trial Chamber heard, for instance, expert Witness Andras Riedlmayer, and witnesses VS-1055 and Safet Sejdic. Regarding the municipality of Mostar, the Chamber refers, inter alia, to 92 quater witness Zoran Tot, and expert Witness Andras Riedlmayer, as well as to exhibits P843, P1044, and P1045 and P1048. Lastly, regarding the municipality of Nevesinje, the Trial Chamber refers, inter alia, to expert Witness Andras Riedlmayer and to witnesses Ibrahim Kujan, Vojislav Dabic, and to Exhibits P524 and P880 under seal. With regard to count 14, looting of non-Serb public or private property as a violation of the laws or customs of war as alleged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber notes that the accused does not challenge the fact that there was looting, but he denies any involvement of SCP/SRS volunteers and claims that he would have condemned such behaviour if it had occurred. The Trial Chamber will now provide examples of evidence it deems sufficient at the 98 bis stage of the proceedings to find that the crimes in count 14 were indeed committed in the various municipalities mentioned in the indictment. Regarding the municipality of Vukovar, the Trial Chamber refers, inter alia, to witnesses VS-002, VS-016 and VS-027. Regarding the municipality of Zvornik, the Trial Chamber refers, inter alia, to witnesses VS-1013, VS-038, VS-1105, and to Exhibits P68, P362, and P521 under seal. Regarding Greater Sarajevo, the Trial Chamber refers to witnesses VS-1111, Safet Sejdic, and to Exhibit P840. Regarding the municipality of Mostar, the Trial Chamber refers to VS-1067, to Witness Vojislav Dabic, and to Exhibits P880 under seal, and P1051 under seal. Finally, regarding the Nevesinje municipality, the Trial Chamber refers, inter alia, to witnesses Ibrahim Kujan and Vojislav Dabic, and to Exhibits P524 and P880 under seal. I'm now going to read out more slowly, because we are moving on to an essential part of the Trial Chamber's decision. The Trial Chamber in the sixth and last section of the instant decision will look into the responsibility of the accused under the heading of instigating. In a preliminary fashion, the Trial Chamber wishes to answer to the accused's argument that he could not be prosecuted before a criminal court of law because the international criminal tribunals and their jurisprudence did not yet exist at the time he gave his speeches. The Trial Chamber finds that this argument is unsustainable. Indeed, the Trial Chamber considers that the accused has a Ph.D. in law, is a former assistant professor in political sciences at the University of Sarajevo and that as such he was bound to know at the time relevant to the indictment, he was bound to know that the prohibition to incite to racial, ethnic, or religious discrimination had been enshrined and codified in international law, inter alia, in Article 7 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of the 10th of December, 1948; in Article 20, paragraph (2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights of 16th of December, 1966. Article 4(a) of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination of 21st of December, 1965, furthermore imposes on states to qualify or characterize as punishable offence, acts of incitement to racial discrimination. The accused was also bound to know that such acts had been punished at the end of the Second World War. Indeed, speeches inciting to discrimination on racial or political grounds had been punished as crimes against humanity by the Nuremberg military tribunal in 1946 in the Streicher decision. The Trial Chamber is therefore of the view that the accused was well aware at the time of the facts he's charged with that there had been already at an international level a criminalisation, a codification into law of incitement to national, racial or religious hatred through propaganda or any other means. The accused could also not ignore -- I'm going slowly because this is really absolutely relevant. He was bound to know that the former SFRY had complied with the obligation to prohibit and punish such discriminatory behaviour by adding Article 134, paragraph 1, to its domestic criminal code. The latter code had been adopted by the Federal Assembly at the session of the federal council held on the 28th of September, 1976, and was later published in the Official Gazette of the 8th of October, 1976. Anyone who is interested, it was issue 44, and it came into force on the 1st of July, 1977. The initial wording of Article 134, when it was adopted in 1977, provided for the offence of incitement a maximum penalty of ten years' of imprisonment. The Trial Chamber notes that this provision was later amended in 1990 and the maximum penalty reduced to five years' of imprisonment. The Trial Chamber finds, therefore, that the accused was aware at the time of the acts he is charged with that it had become, at national level, a federal criminal offence in the former Yugoslavia to incite to national, racial, or religious hatred through propaganda or any other means against peoples and nationals present in the territory of the said country. International criminal tribunals and jurisdiction were created by the Security Council only to replace domestic jurisdiction to punish acts of genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity in a situation of emergency in order to ensure international peace. The principle of nullum crimen sine lege is duly complied with. In order to ascertain whether the accused may be held responsible for the commission of crimes reviewed in part five of this decision, the Trial Chamber must analyse the evidence on record and determine whether this evidence is sufficient for a reasonable Trial Chamber to find that the accused incited or instigated within the meaning of Article 7(1) of the Statute to crimes being committed as alleged in the indictment. In order to do so, the Trial Chamber is going to analyse the evidence it has received with regard to each of the three legal requisite elements of instigation mentioned before, namely, firstly, the existence of one or several acts underlying the charge of instigation to commit the crimes alleged in the indictment. Secondly, the knowledge of the accused of the real likelihood that crimes would be committed further to his acts that were elements of instigation, and for the crime of persecution, his intent to bring about or induce the perpetration of the crime. And thirdly, the existence of a nexus between the acts of the accused and the crimes committed. The Trial Chamber wishes to stress, first of all, that it was not able to at this stage of the proceedings to find that evidence on record were blatantly void of credibility or incapable of belief. First of all, with regard to the first requisite condition of the test, namely the element of instigating, by using the word "instigated," the Prosecution in the indictment generally charges that the accused's speeches, communications, acts, and/or omissions contributed to the perpetrators' decision to commit the crimes alleged and this was confirmed by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Therefore, the Trial Chamber took into account all the acts charged against the accused that may have contributed to or otherwise influenced the decision-making process that drove physical perpetrators to commit the crimes alleged in the indictment. The Trial Chamber thus took into account several acts that can be attributed to the accused and that may have influenced the physical perpetrators of the crimes alleged in the indictment. Firstly, the fact that he promoted his nationalistic ideology by any means possible. For instance, the deportation of non-Serbs, be it directly or through his party the Serbian Chetnik Movement, SCP, and later the SRS party. Secondly, the systematic denigration of non-Serb populations. Thirdly, the spreading of a climate of fear among the Serb and non-Serb populations. Fourthly, the fact he encouraged the SCP/SRS supporters to volunteer, and once they were in the field, to -- of encouraging his supporters to bring about, to implement his nationalistic ideology by any means imaginable. (a), with regard to evidence on promotion by the accused of his nationalistic ideology by all means possible. The Trial Chamber has a large amount of evidence that would make it possible for a reasonable Trial Chamber at the 98 bis stage of the proceedings to find that the accused promoted his nationalistic ideology involving the commission of crimes, including the deportation of non-Serbs either directly or through his party, first the SCP that had been banned, and then through the SRS. The Trial Chamber refers to Exhibit P1278, an article published in the "Politika" daily on 9th of July, 1991, to the effect that the accused had been barred from membership in the Serbian Philosophical Society because on several occasions he had openly advocated violence and hatred, ethnic hatred, as means purported to serve and realise, implement the interests of the Serbian people. The Trial Chamber has received Exhibit P1192, a transcript of a press conference of the 20th of February, 1992, by the accused, which he published in one of his books; the Trial Chamber has received Exhibit P1293, published in the "Politika" newspaper on 2nd of March, 1992; has received P685 under seal, a transcript of various press conferences by the accused between the 26th of March and the 16th of April, 1992, published in one of his books; the Trial Chamber has received P1324, a transcript of a press conference of the 5th of March, 1992, by the accused, published in one of his books. And they show how virulent the accused spoke, notably when he threatened that there may be a bloodbath in Bosnia. The Trial Chamber also refers to Exhibit P1298. That includes also a "Politika" article of the 27th of March, 1992, referring to violent utterances by the accused, who threatened that more blood might be shed if the Muslim fundamentalists were intent on playing with fire. The Trial Chamber refers to Exhibit P1200 that contains, among others, a "Borba" article of the 28th of May, 1992, mentioning some violent words of the accused, notably at an SRS rally in May 1992 in which he summed up the territorial conquests of the Serbian force and insisted on the fact that more still had to be done by "cleansing" the left bank of the Drina River. The Trial Chamber has also received Exhibit P1180, an interview by the accused to the Novi Sad television in June 1991, published in one of his books, in which the accused stated that he had extremely powerful strongholds in north-eastern Bosnia. More specifically he said that the mere fact that in some places the Croats and the Muslims had not been sleeping in their homes for days demonstrates that the SRS/SCP was not as insignificant as it purports to be. The Trial Chamber further refers to Witness Nebojsa Stojanovic, who, in prior witness statements admitted as P526 and P528, testified that the accused thought that Croatia had to be ethnically cleansed and that the borders of Greater Serbia had been to be reclaimed. Witness VS-016 stated, page 11120 of the French transcript, that the accused said as follows: "Not one Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive," at a political rally in Vukovar around mid-November 1991, outside the headquarter of the Leva Supoderica. Witness VS-033, pages 5542 and 5543 of the French transcript, testified that when he was visiting on the ground, the accused urged the volunteers to kill all of the enemies. The Trial Chamber further refers to witness Vesna Bosanac, page 11404 of the French transcript, testified that the accused said on Serb radio that Vukovar had to fall and all its buildings razed to the ground. For her, it meant that the accused was instigating the members of the Serb forces to totally destroy the town and give them free rein to massacre civilians as they pleased. Finally, the Trial Chamber refers to Witness VS-004, page 3376 of the French transcript, who testified that the accused held inflammatory and virulent, unrestrained speeches. This would be relating to evidence on systematic denigration of non-Serb population by the accused. The Trial Chamber has evidence that would make it possible for a reasonable trier of fact to conclude at this stage that the accused denigrated, in a systematic fashion, Croats, Muslims and other non-Serb population through his speeches, by, for instance, calling them "Ustasha" when he spoke of Croats, calling Muslims "Balija." These are extremely degrading and pejorative terms. With regard to the denigration of Croat populations, the Trial Chamber has received Exhibit P34, an interview by the accused to "Politika" in which it can be read the following: "How can anyone negotiate with Ustashas? Haven't you seen that today there are only Ustashas in the Croatian population? There are only very few exceptions." Similarly, in Exhibit P1194, the accused was stating that there were only, and I quote, 16 good Croats, 10 plus 6, 16, which had the right to stay in Serbia. The rest had to be expelled from Serbia. The Trial Chamber can also mention Exhibit P298. It is a Croatian television footage aired on November 7, 1991, as well as Exhibit P1201 corresponding to the transcript of an interview of the accused for the TV show "Politika," broadcast on June 12, 1992. In these sequences, the accused is referring to Vukovar and Hrtkovci as Ustasha strongholds where you can find the worst Ustashas. Another exhibit, Exhibit P1211 corresponding to the transcript of a press conference given by the accused on January 13, 1993, published in one of his books in which the accused speaks, among other things, of an Ustasha-ruled Croatia. Furthermore, Witness VS-007 testified at page 6072 of the French transcript that the accused had used the term "Ustashas" in front of bodies of Croats who had been killed during combat, and at that moment he said they have -- those bodies have to be burned so they don't foul up the air and contaminate us. The Trial Chamber also refers to Witness Goran Stoparic who testified on page 2338 of the French transcript that the accused was generally calling all Croats, Ustashas. Finally, Witness VS-2000 can also be mentioned at pages 13994 to 13995 of the French transcript, because there he mentions the call for vengeance delivered by the accused against Balijas during the speech delivered in Mali Zvornik in 1992. I stop for a minute because it's still freezing in this courtroom. With regard to the fact that the accused would have spread a climate of fear among the civilian population. The Trial Chamber has a number of pieces of evidence that could lead any reasonable trier of fact to infer at this stage that the accused through his speech spread a climate of fear among the civilians. For example, the Trial Chamber has Exhibit P153 corresponding to documents published in the daily "Velika Srbija," issue 9 of 1991, and re-published in one of the accused's books as well as Exhibit P179, which is a video of a speech given by the accused in 1991 in which the accused is referring to the new Ustasha leaders in Croatia who are once again implementing a genocidal policy aimed at the Serbs. The Trial Chamber can also mention Exhibit P35 corresponding to a speech made by the accused on June 4, 1991, in which he said, and I quote: "All those who do not have a clear conscience have good reasons to be afraid of us, the Serbs. They're quite right to fear us. We, the Serbs, throughout history, we forgot too much. We forgave too much. We told the Croats that if they ever resumed their genocidal activities against the Serbs, not only would we avenge every victim, but we would also settle our scores and settle the scores of the victims of World War I and World War II." In Exhibit P62, a documentary film broadcast by the BBC and called "Death of Yugoslavia" aired in March 1995, you hear the accused say, and I quote: "We, the Serbs, are in danger. Croat fascist hordes are attacking Serb women, Serb children. The Croat fascist hordes are planning the genocide of the Serbs." The Trial Chamber can also mention Witness Anthony Oberschall who testified on page 1999 of the French transcript that the terms used for propaganda do not have the same meaning and are used differently in nationalistic speeches than in normal speeches. Furthermore, he also added on page 2123 of the French transcript that the context is absolutely essential to interpret the statement. According to this witness, it is -- it might be allowed to advocate violence in a peaceful situation, but, however, this is absolutely banned in a situation, in a context where civilians are being killed. The Trial Chamber can also mention Witness VS-061. During his testimony on page 10036 of the French transcript, he said that he -- during the speech in Hrtkovci, he heard that the -- the accused was in favour of measures of retorsion against the Croats. All this is corroborated by Katica Paulic who testified at pages 11904 to 11909 of the French transcript that during the Hrtkovci speech, the accused had said that Croats and Hungarians had to leave and that the crowd had reacted very favourably to this speech by chanting, and I quote, "We will kick you out, Ustashas." According to this witness, non-Serbs didn't even dare go to work after this speech. (d) Finally regarding the way the accused encouraged the volunteers of the SRS/SCP so that they would volunteer and that once on the field they would achieve his nationalistic ideology by any means, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that would lead any reasonable trier of fact to conclude at this point of time that the accused directly encouraged his supporters to volunteer, to go and fight, by all means to defend his nationalistic ideas and promote Greater Serbia, which could only come about through the commission of crimes, notably deportation of non-Serbs. The Trial Chamber, for example, has Exhibit P1074 in which Witness Zoran Rankic says that before the volunteers left for the front, the accused would encourage them by telling them be -- "become heroes." "Become heroes," I repeat, and "Fight for Greater Serbia." The Trial Chamber can also mention document P217 in which the accused appoints 16 Chetniks as Vojvodas on May 13, 1993. There's also document P255, a video showing the accused appointing Vojvoda to 18 Chetniks on 31 March 1993, and P218 which also corresponds to another appointment by the accused of several Chetniks as Vojvodas on March 20, 1994. The Trial Chamber also has the testimony of Goran Stoparic, a SRS volunteer, according to which, pages 2337 to 2339 of the French transcript, the accused visited the members of the Leva Supoderica unit in Vukovar, in the presence of officers of the 1st Brigade of the Guards. According to this witness, the accused had come to encourage this unit made up of volunteers of the SRS/SCP, and Goran Stoparic was very glad that he had visited them on the front line. The Trial Chamber can also mention Witness VS-002, according to which -- to whom on pages 6556 and 6557 of the French transcript, the accused was the only political leader who came to see them in Vukovar, a visit for which the fighters were extremely grateful. The Trial Chamber can finally mention Witness Vesna Bosanac on page 11422 of the French transcript. She said that at -- in Vukovar she heard the accused encourage soldiers, be it volunteers or members of other units, and she said that the accused was the ideological leader and people would do what he said. (2), regarding the second condition for instigation relating to the awareness the accused had of the real likelihood that crimes would result from his instigation as regards crimes referred to in counts 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 and relating to his criminal intent to provoke or induce the commission of crime regarding persecution as alleged in count 1, the Trial Chamber has an amount of evidence that could lead any reasonable trier of fact to conclude is that the accused continued with his violent propaganda even though, (a), he was aware of the influence he had on Serbian public opinion in general and on his supporters and volunteers of the SCP/SRS more specifically. (b) He was aware that there was a war waging at the time and that this made his instigation extremely dangerous. (c) He was aware that in times of war crimes are committed. (d) He was aware or could not ignore the notorious criminal history of some of these Serbian volunteers and therefore the very high risk that these volunteers could -- would commit crimes of war once given weapons and in -- with this war raging. (e) He was fully aware of what was happening on the ground and the fact that crimes were being committed against civilian populations in the combat zones where the volunteers of the SCP/SRS were sent. (f) He had the mens rea to entice his listeners, and particularly, his volunteers into persecuting non-Serb population for political and religious reasons. Moving to (a). First, regarding the awareness that the accused had of the influence he had on Serb public opinion in general, on the supporters of his ideology and volunteers of the SCP/SRS in particular. I will now develop what has been mentioned earlier, and this will take some time. The Trial Chamber here refers itself to Exhibit P1337. It is the foreword written by the accused on September 24, 2002 and published in his book "Ideology of Serbian nationalism." In this foreword the accused states and I quote: "Passive spectators are all potential fighters. You only need to enlighten them, to teach them, to give them a nationalist orientation, to raise their patriotic awareness and to give them the love of the land, of the homeland. Propaganda is based on the fact that -- that a great majority of people naturally are ready to gullibly believe everything they read, hear, or see on television." This can be found in the accused's book. In Exhibit P1264, which corresponds to Articles of the daily "Velika Srbija" dated 15 August, 1990, and reproduced in one of the accused's book, he says on page 25, and I quote: "We now have a very powerful weapon in our hands, the daily 'Velika Srbija'" which proves that the accused was well aware that the circulation of his ideologies through this daily would have a very strong impact on the Serbian public opinion and more --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had to intervene here, because we have an interpreter here who gives false interpretation, and this was a good time to intervene when he said that we had powerful army. You didn't say powerful army. You said powerful weapon and that that weapon was the Greater Serbia. You are bringing this interpreter on purpose, this interpreter against whom I have intervened a number of times. I have listened to everything you have been saying so far with great enjoyment, and this overjoyed me, but here I had to intervene because this is a bit too much now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind the interpreters that they have to be -- I know it's a very difficult job, but they have to be as close as possible to the French that's being read. A weapon is not an army, and so forth and so on. Let me backtrack a little, which -- so that I can read again what I read properly in French and was misinterpreted. In -- in Exhibit P1264 corresponding to Articles of the daily "Velika Srbija" of August 15, 1990 and reproduced in one of the books of the accused, the accused says on page 25, and I quote, and I am quoting exactly what I read earlier: "We now have a powerful weapon in our hands, the daily 'Velika Srbija,'" which shows that the accused was aware that the circulation of his ideology through this daily would have a very strong impact on Serbian public opinion and more especially on the volunteers of the SCP, and later on the volunteers of the SRS. In Exhibit P1220 is an interview of the accused by a Japanese journalist, dated May 18, 1993, and printed in one of the books of the accused. On page 2, the accused says that he has a great political influence in Bosnia and thousands of Serbian volunteers listen to him and that he has influence over the thousands of Serbian fighters and that should there be any foreign military intervention, his influence would only be greater. On page 12 of the same document, P1220, the accused recognises that his party is extremely popular and says that this explains why he is so popular, especially since he always speaks his mind, contrary to other politicians. Similarly, the video footage corresponding to items P70 and P339 illustrate the popularity of the accused and the effect his speeches used to have his on listeners in general and notably on his volunteers. Furthermore the Trial Chamber can mention witnesses Nebojsa Stojanovic, paragraph 6 of his preliminary statement admitted as P527; Goran Stoparic, pages 2442 and 2443 of the French transcript; VS-016, pages 11120, 11171 and 11181 of the French transcript; Aleksa Ejic, page 10343 of the French transcript or VS-061, page 9924 of the French transcript, in light of which it appears that the words uttered by the accused had a great impact on those listening, and hearing them, hearing these words. Now, (b) -- Judge Lattanzi asks me to slow down. So (b), regarding the awareness of the accused as far as the fact that there was a war raging at the time. Given the different -- all the evidence already mentioned in this decision, the Trial Chamber will only give one example for this regarding the conflict-ridden background of these crimes. Exhibit P1205 is a transcript of an interview made by the accused for the Pale TV station, aired in September 1992, in which the accused states on page 4 about the war in Bosnia that it is both a religious and a civil war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now continue, and we will soon have a break. (c) Regarding the fact that the accused was aware that in times of war crimes are committed. The Trial Chamber will not expound on this since the accused is not challenging the fact and even admitted this during the 98 bis hearing at pages 16645 and 16658 of the French transcript. (d), regarding the fact that the accused was aware of the criminal record of a number Serbian volunteers and their -- these volunteers, once equipped with weapon, could very well commit crimes of war. The Trial Chamber has evidence which would lead any reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the accused was aware of the criminal past of some of the volunteers or at least could not ignore this criminal past. In this respect, the Trial Chamber mentions Exhibit P836, which is the statement of Matija Boskovic, a 92 quater witness. In this statement, the witness says that when the war started, criminals were released and joined volunteer units. According to Witness Zoran Rankic, paragraph 35 of his preliminary statement, Exhibit P74, it was public knowledge at the time that the authorities were releasing people from gaol and that the SRS war headquarters never checked whether the volunteers that the SCP/SRS were sending to the front had any criminal records. According to this witness, this had no importance for the accused. I will -- we will have our break in a minute. It will be a 20-minute break, and we will resume at 12.30. I will still have ten pages to read of this decision, then I will start reading the beginning of my opinion. We will stop around 1.30 for an hour break so that the accused and everyone in the room can have lunch, and then we can resume the reading at 2.30, nonstop to 7.00, hoping to finish earlier, so that my opinion can be fully read. This being said, Judge Harhoff just told me that in the afternoon -- no, obviously he can stay. Mr. Seselj, we're going to have a break, so please be brief.
