utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, most of the time the three Judges on this Bench, I will repeat this later, they usually sit on two trials, and usually for lunch, you know, we just have a glass of water. We'll have a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. First, let me tell you for that for administrative reasons I told you that we will have an hour break for lunch, but we'll have an hour and a half. Secondly, I was told that the interpreters cannot work more than six hours in a row, and because of this they cannot work any longer than six hours at a time. Furthermore, because of the financial resources in this Tribunal, you know that this Tribunal is on its way -- is going to finish, and because of that we do not have an additional team of interpreters. Therefore, once we will have finished with the six hours of interpretation, we will as to have and we will resume tomorrow as of 2.15. Therefore, I will be able to finish the ten pages left in this decision, then start to read the beginning of my opinion. We will resume this afternoon, and once the six hours are up, we will stop for the day. I will continue reading, page 40. (e) Finally, regarding the fact that the accused was aware of what was happening on the ground and aware of the crimes committed in the combat zones where the volunteers of the SRS/SCP were sent. First as to what the accused knew about what was happening on the ground. The Chamber can use the testimony of Goran Stoparic, pages 2337 to 2340 of the French transcript; of Mladen Kulic, page 4455 of the French transcript; Witness VS-002, pages 6555 and 6556 of the French transcript; VS-04, pages 3413 of the French transcript; and page VS-007, pages 6069 and 6070 of the French transcript which all address visits made by the accused to the field. Similarly, for example, in Exhibit P1207, corresponding to interviews of the accused, dated November 26, 1992, and printed into one of his books, in Exhibit P1204 corresponding to an interview of the accused of September 1992, also printed in one of his books, and in Exhibit P1221 corresponding to an interview of the accused dated May 21, 1993, also printed in one of his books, we find a description of three visits and inspections by the accused of SCP/SRS units headed by the three following Vojvodas: Branislav Gavrilovic, Vasilije Vidovic, as well as Slavko Aleksic. Now, as regards the awareness the accused had of the crimes committed in the combat zones where the volunteers of the SCP/SRS were present. The Trial Chamber can quote, for instance, Witness VS-033 who stated on pages 5524, 5525, 5529 and 533 -- 5531 of the transcript in French that in Vocin, Novacic had discovered that criminals were present among the volunteers and had complained about it to the Main Staff of the SRS. This witness, in addition, ascertained that Novacic had telephone contacts with the representatives of the war headquarters of the SRS every two to three days or he went himself to Belgrade and reported directly to the accused. The Chamber can also quote Exhibit P1191 which is a press conference of the accused on the 23rd of January, 1992, and reproduced in one of his books in which the accused indicates that his volunteers were in permanent contact with the leadership of the SCP/SRS and forwarded information from the front line. The Chamber holds that the evidence it has could enable a reasonable Judge to infer that the accused knew or could not ignore that crimes had been committed in the combat areas where the volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS had been sent. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber holds that it has sufficient evidence at this stage to allow a reasonable Judge to conclude that the accused was aware of the likelihood of the crimes being committed following these acts of instigation. (f), as regards the intent of the accused to provoke or entice his audience to persecute the non-Serb population on political or religious grounds, the Chamber refers to first of all to the evidence mentioned in the above on systematic denigration of the non-Serb population by the accused and on the promotion of the accused of a nationalistic view by the commission of these crimes mentioned in the above. The Chamber then refers to the various evidence relating to the spreading by the accused of a climate of fear among the civilian population. The Chamber holds that the accused, through his speeches, instilled this fear with the aim of provoking the Serbs, volunteers or civilians, to persecute the Croats amongst others, to defend the so-called genocidal policy against the Serbian people established by the Croat leaders at the time. In this. Regard, the Chamber has, for instance, the testimony of Katica Paulic, who recounted on page 11904 of the transcript in French that the accused at a rally in Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, 1992, took the floor and singled out Serb members in the audience from other ethnic communities and by disseminating an anti-Croat feeling. According to this witness, on page 11905 of the transcript in French, the words of accused disseminating his discriminatory intent galvanised the people in the audience, who then started shouting, inter alia, "Ustasha, we will kick you out. We will kick you out, Ustasha." Then Aleksa Ejic indicates, on page 10343 of the transcript in French, that the crowd on that day gave the accused an ovation when he hinted that the Croats should return to their nice homeland. The Chamber may also rely on Exhibit P548 which is a note from the Sremska Mitrovica state security department centre testifying to the fact that the accused had taken the floor whilst the crowd was agitating and spouting slogans such as, "Ustasha out. This is Serbia. There is no place for Croats in Serbia." The Chamber refers to the prior statement of Witness Jelena Radosevic, also admitted under Exhibit P580, in which the latter states that the accused had come to Vocin at the end of November and the beginning of December 1991 to fuel tensions with a view to speeding up the departure of the Croats from the town. The Chamber holds that this visit by the accused is part of a campaign of persecution against the non-Serb population as mentioned, amongst others, by the witness Fadil Banjanovic, VS-1064, and VS-1066. The Chamber can also quote Exhibit number P547 that concerns the speech of the accused in Hrtkovci and reproduced in one of his books in which he refers to the Ustashas and calls for the expulsions of non-loyal Croats because there is no place for them in Srem. He continues by saying that if they did not leave of their own free will, they would be taken by force and put on board buses until the borders or up to the borders of the Serb territory. This scenario mentioned by the accused implies the participation of the volunteers and Serb civilian population to -- in the -- sorry in the accomplishment of this criminal purpose. Lastly, the Chamber noted Exhibit P1197, which is a transcript of a televised interview of the accused given to TV studio and broadcast on the 8th of April, 1992, which was reproduced in one of the books of the accused. The accused asserts in that book that he has never met a good Croat and that the Croats are the enemies of the Serbs and the worst criminals ever. On several occasions, he uses the word "Ustasha," which is a derogatory term, and proclaims that the expulsion of the Croats must be done once and for all, for if they stayed, the situation would be all the more unstable. I shall now move on to my third point. As regards the third condition of instigation, namely the existence of a substantial nexus between instigation and the crimes, the Trial Chamber has received evidence allowing a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the accused exercised a determining influence over the perpetrators of the crime because of the recruitment and the sending of volunteers through the SRS/SCP in the localities in which they were and were therefore able to commit the crimes alleged in the indictment, and because of the moral authority he exercised over his volunteers, which was considerable, and on all the sympathisers of his nationalistic ideology, since some men proclaimed they were Seselj's men or Chetniks, the Trial Chamber notes in this regard that evidence indicates that the SCP/SRS had not taken the trouble to train the volunteers in combat or humanitarian law matters before sending them off to join the army. The Chamber feels that the audience of the accused was broader and encompassed not only the volunteers that had been recruited by the SCP/SRS but also all the sympathisers of his nationalistic ideology. However for -- in light of judicial economy, the Trial Chamber will provide examples of this evidence that testify to that: (a), the recruitment and sending volunteers on the front line by the SCP/SRS headed by the accused; (b), the considerable moral authority of the accused over these volunteers; and lastly, (c), the commission of crimes in the indictment by volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS or sympathisers of this organisation. I shall now review these last sections (a), (b), (c), in detail. Now, (a), as regards evidence pertaining to the recruitment and the sending of volunteers on the front line by the SCP/SRS headed by the accused. The Chamber can, for instance, quote Exhibit P1233 which is an interview given by the accused to Radio Loznica on the 10th of November, 1993, and reproduced in one of his books in which the accused talks about the way in which he contributed to the attack on Zvornik. He states, and I'm going to quote the words of accused: "You should know that our volunteers have fought together with a special unit of the Serb Ministry of the Interior and it is thanks to this coordinated action that Zvornik was liberated on time." Likewise, in Exhibit P342 which is a video of an interview by the accused, dated 1994, the accused states that he sent at least 30.000 armed volunteers on all the battle-fields where the Serbian people was fighting. In Exhibit P30, which is an excerpt from a BBC documentary, "Death of Yugoslavia," broadcast in March 1995, in which the accused is interviewed, we see the accused saying, we hear the accused saying, I quote: "In 1991, we started organising the volunteers in a big way and sending them on the front lines that had already been drawn up, including in Eastern Slavonia." The recruitment of volunteers by the SCP/SRS and sending on the front line from October 1991 onwards is also mentioned by Witness VS-033 who specified during his testimony on page 5505 that he had decided to volunteer for the SCP/SRS, which was sending volunteers on the front line. The witness also indicated that registration as a volunteer automatically meant becoming a member of the Serbian Radical Party. Witness VS-038 indicated on pages 10195 and 10196 that the -- that recruitment was done through propaganda in the media where the representative of the SRS, including the accused, called on the patriots to defend the Serbian people. Witness VS-0158 also explained in his prior statement, tendered into evidence under Exhibit number P1053 under seal, that at the beginning of 1995 he had been visited in the cafe where he worked by several members of the SRS and that these men had asked him to join a group of the SCP/SRS volunteers. The witness accepted and decided to join the SRS. (b) As regards the moral authority. The considerable moral authority the accused had over his volunteers. The Chamber has evidence which would allow any reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the accused exercised a determining influence over the SCP/SRS volunteers sent off to the front line. In addition to the evidence relating to the overall influence of the accused on the SRS and SCP sympathisers and the volunteers recruited by SCP/SRS, already mentioned in the second part of the second condition for instigation the Chamber can also quote Witness Fadil Kopic who stated on page 5913 of the French transcript that the SCP/SRS volunteers viewed the accused as a god. Furthermore, the Chamber can also quote Witness VS-0092 who stated during his testimony before the Chamber on page 6557 of the French transcript concerning the accused, "He was a Serb Vojvoda. We would never have dismissed his orders." Lastly, (c), as regards the commission of crimes by the SCP/SRS volunteers or sympathisers of the accused's ideology, the Trial Chamber has evidence which would entitled a reasonable trier of fact to conclude that the volunteers recruited by SCP/SRS committed the alleged crimes in the various counts of the indictment. We shall address these counts each in turn. Count 4, murder. The Chamber may quote, for instance, Witness VS-016 who mentioned during his testimony before the Chamber on page 11137 of the French transcript murders committed in Ovcara by several volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS identified by name. Or Witness VS-007 who indicated on page 6103 and 6104 of the French transcript that he heard that volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS, namely the Kinez and the Kameni groups, who, for the most part, were very dangerous and brutal, participated in the executions of non-Serb civilians in Ovcara. The Chamber remarks that the presence in the municipality of Vukovar of a unit of volunteers of SCP/SRS placed under the command of Milan Lancuzanin aka Kameni is confirmed by Witness VS-002, on pages 6535 and 6536 of the French transcript. Counts 8 and 9, on torture and cruel treatment. The Chamber can, for instance, quote witness VS-1013, who on page 5248 of the French transcript states that Cele, the head of a Seselj's men unit mistreated and killed detainees. The Chamber notes that Exhibit number P217 says that Cele was a volunteer that had been recruited by the SCP/SRS, who was proclaimed Vojvoda by the accused on the 13th of May, 1993. Witness VS-1013 mentions also on page 5257 of the French transcript that he heard that sexual assaults committed at the cultural centre of Celopek in the municipality of Zvornik had been committed by a volunteer nicknamed Repic and his team. The Chamber notes that Witness Asim Alic on pages 7002 to 7004, 7007 and 7022 of the French transcript confirmed the presence of volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS in the municipality of Zvornik who had substantial military equipment and identity papers showing that they were members to the SCP -- they were members of the SCP and/or the SRS. Among these people were two brothers originating from the suburbs of Belgrade called Vukovic and nicknamed Repic, as regards the last one, the youngest one. Counts 10 and 11 relating to deportation and forcible transfer as an inhumane act. The Chamber refers for instance to Aleksa Ejic who on page 10382 recounts that Rade Cakmak, who introduced himself as a member of the SRS, participated in acts of violence against the inhabitants of Hrtkovci and settled with his family in a house belonging to a Hungarian. Fourth point, count 12, wanton destruction of villages and devastation not justified by military necessity. The Chamber can quote Witness VS-1067, who states on page 15287, 15315, 15316 of the French transcript, as in paragraph 78 of his prior statement admitted under Exhibit number P1051 under seal -- under -- that a group of -- of 50 or 60 men who introduced themselves as members of the SRS and that had as their main commander Vojislav Seselj, arrived in April 1992 in Bjelusine, in the municipality of Mostar and that in April 1992 this group went towards the village of Topla, located a kilometre and a half away from Bjelusine, that he saw Seselj's men driving the population out and looting the houses and burning them afterwards. The Chamber can also quote 92 quater witness Matija Boskovic, a volunteer member of the SCP/SRS who indicates in paragraph 27 of his prior statement admitted under Exhibit number P836 that his unit burnt some houses in the village of Dugi Dio, located in the municipality of Zvornik. Fifth point, count 13, destruction or wilful damage of institutions dedicated to education or religion. The Chamber can quote Witness VS-1055, for instance, who states on pages 7805, 7810, 7812, 7846 of the French transcript that at the end of March or at the beginning of April, 1992, armed group headed by Vasilije Vidovic, nicknamed Vaske, were present in the town of Ilijas in the area of Sarajevo. These men were wearing various insignia, traditionally the hallmark of a Chetnik organisation. Skulls and bones, cockade, fur hat, the traditional Serb headgear or sajkaca. The witness in addition recognised the insignia of the SRS on the headgear and the subara of Vaske's men. In addition, he said that he had heard from the Serbs living in Ilijas that Vaske was one of the men responsible for the destruction of the religious buildings in the town. The Chamber can also quote 92 quater witness Mujo Dzafic, who in paragraph 24 of his prior statement, admitted under Exhibit Number P284, that Vaske destroyed all the religious buildings, mosques, and churches around Ilijas, including the Stari Ilijas mosque. Six point, count 14, plunder of public and private -- or private property. The Chamber may quote Witness Nebojsa Stojanovic, who in paragraphs 15 to 16 of his prior statement, admitted under Exhibit P57, that he saw the looting of the houses in Desna Supoderica by volunteers recruited by the SCP/SRS who among other things found it amusing to defecate everywhere in the houses. The Chamber can also quote 92 quater witness Mujo Dzafic, who states in paragraph 31 of his prior statement, admitted under P840, that a short while before the end of the war, Vaske and his men looted all the companies in Ilijas by taking away building materials which they then loaded on lorries. The witness saw Vaske taking charge of a lorry which was filled with stolen goods. Fifth point, count 1, persecution on political, racial, religious grounds. The Chamber refers inter alia to all the aforementioned evidence regarding the other counts mentioned in the indictment that constitute some of the underlying acts of persecution committed on religious and political grounds with the participation of the accused. It is therefore not necessary to provide further evidence that the Chamber has relating to this count that enable us to establish a nexus between instigation and this crime. Accordingly the Trial Chamber feels that there is sufficient evidence for a reasonable trier of fact to conclude at this stage that there is a substantial nexus between the acts of instigations by the accused and the crimes committed. Conclusion. In light of the review of evidence on the commission of crimes on the participation of the accused in such a commission, through instigating acts and on the nexus between the crimes and the instigating acts of the accused, the Chamber holds that there is sufficient evidence at this stage to meet the requirements of Rule 98 bis of the Rules for a reasonable trier of fact to convict the accused beyond all reasonable doubt for having instigated the commission of all the crimes alleged in the nine counts of the indictment. The Chamber in its majority, Judge Antonetti dissenting, wishes to recall that this conclusion does not require the Chamber at this stage to review all other forms of responsibility alleged in the indictment, namely the physical commission, specifically persecution, expulsion, and -- deportation and forcible transfers, participation in a joint criminal enterprise, and the other forms of responsibility as provided for in Article 7(1) of the Statute. For the foregoing reasons and pursuant to Rule 98 bis of the Rules, the Chamber in its -- the Chamber dismisses the accused's motion. Since I do not agree with part of the majority decision, I must state my position orally. In light of the issues that will be raised, while I read out [Realtime transcript read in error "redact"] my text, I shall use charts which will be displayed at my request on the various screens. I would like to thank the Registrar and the usher in advance for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the method I have used to reach these conclusions which are my personal conclusions, I want to first and foremost express my thanks to our intern and to my legal assistant who made it possible to prepare the chart that is soon to be presented. It was a lot of work, because they had to go through thousands and documents and tens of thousands of pages to do so. It was a major piece of work, a major undertaking, and I wanted to thank them for this. In order to assess the Prosecution evidence, first of all, by way of introduction, I wish to say that I relied mainly on an exhibit that I feel is very important that was tendered into evidence by the OTP that is now part of the case file and that relates to all the interviews or transcripts of the accused until the Milosevic proceedings. It went over several days, and it is several hundred pages long. So this was one of the foundations on which I relied. Equally, I read and scrutinised each and every decision by Trial Chambers and Appeals Chambers in relation to the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia, and these are res judicata. These are of common notice, and I may state some of them in my dissenting opinion. And apart from the documents, I also read motions and public decisions in cases that were relevant to the matters at issue in this case. When I finish reading my partly dissenting opinion, which is 73 pages long, I'll give to Mr. Marcussen and Mr. Seselj the document I'm about to read out, together with attached charts and tables listing witnesses and exhibits so that they could find their way around, as it were. First of all, I have structure, a plan. Mr. Usher, please display it on the ELMO. It has been translated into English and into the accused's language. So you can see this in English. I will have some preliminary remarks, then the 98 bis proceedings in relation to acquittal. Third chapter, the crimes alleged in the indictment, allegedly committed in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Serbia. The fourth chapter, individual criminal responsibility as to planning ordering, instigating, committing, under JCE I, II, and III, crimes of persecutions, crimes of deportation, and of forcible transfer. Aiding and abetting under number 5. And finally, the charges with two overall charts summing up the counts which in my view should give rise to acquittal, in part, of the accused and summing up the counts that -- for which the trial proceedings should be continued. I have a few minutes left before the break, and I'll start with chapter 1 -- or, rather, with preliminary remarks. Review of Prosecution evidence further to Rule 98 bis. It's to be seen here in a very specific context compared with other cases brought before this Tribunal. First of all, the pre-trial custody is really out of the ordinary. The accused was detained on the 24th of February, 2003. This pre-trial and trial custody has lasted more than eight years, way beyond the standards set up by the European Court of Human Rights, and it may only be extended for relevant and sufficient grounds, such as the complexity of the case, the need to maintain the accused at the disposal of justice, the need to prevent re-offending. See on this point European Court of Human Rights 29th of October, 2009, the Paradysz v. France case. Another reason may be the issue of pressure exerted on witnesses. In this regard refer to the European Court of Human Rights, 10th of March, 2009, Bykov v. Russia. Secondly, there have been several ongoing allegations that result from the unlawful disclosure of the names of protected witnesses or from pressure exerted on witnesses. The possible impact of such allegations on the indictment were, in my view anyway, nonexistent because pressure or disclosure of names of protected witnesses did not occur before the indictment was drafted. The indictment was therefore not contaminated by this type of pressure or violation, if any. Thirdly, there are ongoing contempt proceedings against several OTP members. In my view, such proceedings in which we can only expect the conclusions of the amicus curiae at best in October 2011 may have a direct impact on the indictment in the event that witness interviews would have been vitiated, invalidated, by such pressure exerted on them. Since an indictment is based on interviews, witness interviews that gave rise to witness statements that are then admitted into evidence, you have, for instance, the statements of witness VS-009 of 12 February 2003 and 16th of June, 2006, but it relies also on documents, therefore there may be an impact, such as to carry out the total or partial nullity of the indictment. Therefore, I believe at my own level that in any event it would be better to wait until October before we can usefully start the second main stage of the proceedings further to Rule 73. Should the amicus curia conclude that there was no contempt of court, should he exonerate the OTP, the Defence case could then commence. Conversely, no Defence case can begin before the total or partial cleansing of the indictment, be it on application of the Prosecution, further to Rule 51 in relation to the withdrawal of an indictment, or at the request of the accused, further to Rule 73. In the latter case, the accused could seize the Chamber for a decision to be issued or to obtain reparation of the damage suffered. Furthermore, this would be a first in this Tribunal, and since this -- such a case was never envisioned by the Rules, I am of the view that the Trial Chamber, proprio motu, failing motions by the parties and further to Rule 85(A), could decide that all the evidence has been adduced and start the end of the proceedings as per Rule 86. I have two and a half pages left. We will finish the day at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am absolutely opposed to this request by the Prosecutor, because I never ever filed a confidential submission. I filed a public motion, and it can be seen on my website, and it was also published in one of my books. So it can under no circumstances be a confidential motion. It is me who decides whether my motions are confidential or public, and I'm fully opposed to this manipulation by Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will see whether there's a need for redaction or not, whatever the case may be. Let me say that at this stage of the proceedings it is not necessary to look into whether there was one or several cases of perjury. As far as I can see, it's only at the time of the final deliberation that this issue will have to be settled in a final way. In this respect, I must remind you of a very recent decision of the Appeals Chamber dated 1st of April, 2011, in the case this, Tharcisse Renzaho. Paragraph 196: It says that the Defence must prove that the damage suffered is tantamount to an error of law invalidating the judgement. Well, the President has not ruled yet on the new submission, so we have to wait for his decision. This submission does not bear any direct bearing, be it direct or indirect, on the development of the 98 bis proceedings. It would be a totally different kettle of fish if we were at the level of the final deliberations. Finally, this case is to be seen in a very specific context. Inasmuch as we have two Judges of the Bench who also sit in Trial Chambers seized of identical facts for certain crimes or of the same joint criminal enterprise. In these other cases, there are various Prosecution expert witnesses or witnesses who may have witness -- testified in the three cases, or at least two of them, before the same Judges. Each testimony has to be ascertained as to their relevance and probative value at the moment of the final deliberations. Taking into account the fact that the three trials in question are not at the same level of progress, it may be that one Judge may assess the testimony of a given witness in a specific way in one trial, and then he will have to assess the same testimony but several months later in another case without any new element. So is he or she going to give the same probative value, the same weight? The fact that several Judges may participate in several trial proceedings where you hear the same witnesses, this has been dealt with in the Tharcisse Renzaho case, with regard to the second ground of appeal. I think it's interesting enough for me to mention it. And the Appeals Chamber ruled in paragraphs 22 and 23 in the following way: A presumption of impartiality is granted to the Judge in the absence of any contrary evidence, thus dismissing the Defence argument that the same Judges had taken part in other trial proceedings on the same facts with the same witnesses and this would have been a violation of the presumption of innocence. At this stage, notwithstanding the above-mentioned appeals decision, I cannot assess what the direct consequences would be on this case of the fact that my colleagues are part of other cases. This can only be done at the time of the final deliberations, and it might be interesting to hear the parties on this, so much so that I think we have to point out something that must have escaped the Prosecution, namely, that in the indictment against Seselj, the joint criminal enterprise is alleged to end in September 1993, mentioning among the participants Karadzic, whilst in the indictment against Karadzic, Seselj is alleged to be a participant, but the joint criminal enterprise is ongoing from October 1991 to the 30th of November, 1995. There is, therefore, an obvious contradiction that puts the Judge sitting in the two cases in a particularly difficult situation to assess the scope, the extent, of the JCE. To get out of this dilemma, one have -- one would have to wait until the three trials are completed if we want to avoid running this type of risk. The completion strategy of this Tribunal doesn't make it possible to extend trial proceedings forever. All the more so since the accused has been in custody for too long already. Therefore, I had -- I was bound out of principle to raise this theoretical issue at this stage of the proceedings, while saying, much to my regret, that this trial should be completed as quickly as possible, whilst the very implementation of specific inescapable legal constraints should be such that we have to wait until the Karadzic and Stanisic/Zupljanin proceedings are completed to have our final deliberations which should be postponed sine die. So we're going to wait, but there may be a discussion on the redactions. The majority opinion, and me dissenting, decided to redact the part as suggested by Mr. Marcussen.

Your Honours, did you declare this motion of mine to be confidential, and are you entitled to do that? You're not, and this is an abuse of your judicial role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Chapter 2, 98 bis proceedings, acquittal. I'm not going to return, revisit some important parts that have been mentioned, addressed, in the majority decision, but I must remind you that pursuant to the former wording as amended, before it was amended on the 17th November, 1999, an accused may file a motion for acquittal on one or several of the offences in the indictment within seven days following the close of the Prosecution case, and at any rate, before the beginning of the Defence case further to Rule 85(a)(ii). (b) If the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the evidence adduced is not enough to sustain a conviction for this or these charges, it enters a judgement of acquittal at the request of the accused or proprio motu. The way this former wording was used by Trial Chambers has given rise to very long, very lengthy written decisions, sometimes with dissenting opinions and the filing and filings with the Appeals Chamber. It was a time-consuming procedure, and it was likely to delay the proceedings. Therefore, a reform was introduced in 2004 under the incentive of the President of the Tribunal. It aimed at speeding up the procedure by turning the procedure from a written to an oral procedure. And the text -- the wording as adopted is as follows: "At the close of the Prosecution case, the Trial Chamber must -- shall by oral decision after hearing the oral submissions of the parties enter a judgement of acquittal on any count if there is no evidence capable of supporting a conviction." The 98 bis proceedings because of the amendment of this Rule in 2004, does not make it possible, because it is an oral decision, because it is an oral opinion, doesn't make it possible to really go into details with very specific and exact references, as was done before with written decisions. As it is forensically impossible to go into further detail, I cannot review each and every crime to try and identify its possible perpetrator. At this stage, I can only conclude that the author is alleged to be part of the Serb forces without any further specifications. The Serb forces are collectively defined as members of regular units of local TO, often from local TOs, from members of paramilitaries, Arkan's men, Yellow Wasp, White Bees, Seselj's men, or other volunteers without specifying whether these are volunteers affiliated to a political party like to the Serbian Radical Party. The majority opinion is that it is not possible to enter a judgement of partial acquittal based on the wording of this Rule. I disagree totally with their interpretation, all the more so since I'm the coauthor, together with another Judge, of the very wording of the new Rule. The purpose of this reform was never to make it impossible to enter a decision of partial acquittal. It would have been paradoxical that the very purpose of this reform, which is to gain time, actually would have reached the opposite result on the very ground that it is not possible to enter a decision of partial acquittal. It would be equally paradoxical to force the accused to adduce evidence whilst for specific counts or parts of counts the Prosecutor did not lead any evidence or because the evidence they have adduced is not sufficient. This being so, unlike the majority opinion, I am of the view that it was possible for the Trial Chamber to make a decision of acquittal in part or total. Furthermore, the English and French versions are authoritative. In French the fact that you use the term of "Chef d'accusations," count, instead of "infraction," offence, semantically boils down to one and the same thing, because a crime is an element of an offence, an ingredient of an offence or a count. The fact that later on after this amendment was made there was no partial acquittal does not mean this was impossible. It's just that Trial Chambers did not look into the matter or did not want to. The Rule 98 bis proceedings, because it takes place at the close of the Defence case and before -- of the Prosecution case and before the Defence case is very similar to the no-case-to-answer motions of the common law time where there is a motion for acquittal for insufficient Prosecution evidence and the Defence does not respond to that, does not reply. Although the fundamental concept behind Rule 98 bis has been borrowed from common law, this Rule has to be read in its own context in the light of the Statute and the Rules. Therefore there may be discrepancies between the way the Tribunal applies it and the way it is applied in common law systems, in common law jurisdictions. For instance, as to the notion of the legal test to grant a motion further to Rule 98 bis. The Trial Chamber Judge, as mentioned by the Appeals Chamber jurisprudence since their appeals judgement in case the Prosecutor against Jelisic, must assess whether the Judge will enter a conviction beyond any reasonable doubt given the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. This is what the Trial Chamber said, and I will quote: "The Trial Chamber -- the Prosecution submits that when the Trial Chamber required the guilt to be established beyond any reasonable doubt after the presentation of its case, it applied a criteria different and stricter than the one required by law. In its point of view, it would have -- what should have been done was to check whether the evidence, once admitted, had allowed a reasonable tribunal to decide whether the accused is guilty. The question is not to know whether given the evidence adduced the accused should be found guilty but whether he could be found guilty." The jurisprudence of this Tribunal regarding the implementation of Rule 98 bis of the Rules has constantly indicated that Judges must enter an acquittal if the evidence adduced by the Prosecution would not allow any reasonable Judge beyond any reasonable doubt to find the accused guilty. Why is it that in common law there was this need to qualify the Judge as reasonable? By definition, a Judge should not be unreasonable, and the Judge should not be incompetent nor should he be unbiased. However, in common law, these terms were found, "reasonable Judge." Similarly, why is there this addition of "beyond any reasonable doubt"? Beyond any reasonable doubt is the criteria that is required for evidence in an adversarial criminal trial, which means that the evidence adduced by the Prosecution must prove, inasmuch as there can be no doubt in the mind of a reasonable Judge, that the accused is indeed guilty. Now, this notion of a reasonable Judge refers to a legal fiction. It is a standard used to measure the behaviour of an individual. This standard is used in common law, in tort law, notably, to determine whether there has been a violation of the duty of care. Here this duty of care is similar to the notion of "bon pere de famille" in French. This is a very abstract individual seen as the behavioural standard used to measure the behaviour of a given person in order determine whether an offence has been committed and whether -- and to what extent. This notion of reasonable Judge, therefore, refers to a yardstick used to measure how the Judge can appreciate a reasonable doubt. Now, the content of this notion of reasonable doubt in a criminal trial is, because of the bias it adduces, very uncertain. This notion in the United States is seen as a fundamental guarantee for the rights of the accused, whereas in England it has been abandoned or quasi-abandoned in criminal cases. In principle, whenever a Judge has a doubt, the accused must be given the benefit of this doubt so the terms "beyond any reasonable doubt" create, according to me, a greater standard. I -- it seems to me that the Judge must be convinced without a single hesitation that the accused could be found guilty after the evidence has been analysed. Therefore, the case law of this Tribunal is extremely strict. The point here is not to examine the evidence prima facie but to examine the substance of things with -- with all the -- with everything that should be used to appreciate the elements -- the evidence. In a word, it's not -- we're not here just to note facts or to say that facts have happened, we have to explain why and what are the probative evidence adduced by the Prosecution which could allow a reasonable Judge to enter a conviction. Similarly, to make its decision, the Trial Chamber must determine whether for each elements of the crime they are elements where at their highest value could possibly satisfy this Trial Chamber beyond any reasonable doubt that the accused is indeed guilty. The Trial Chamber has on several occasions had the opportunity to rule on these motions and to enter judgements of partial acquittals. In other cases, the Trial Chambers just dismissed these motions. As far as partial acquittal is concerned, I could quote the decision of April 6, 2000, in the Kordic and Cerkez case; the -- the decision of February 28, 2002, in the Martinovic/Naletilic case; the decision of November 28, 2003, in the Brdjanin case; the decision of June 16, 2004, in the Slobodan Milosevic case; and the decision of September 27, 2004, in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. Partial acquittal is possible in law, because it corresponds to the spirit and the letter of Rule 98 bis. Why should an accused, while presenting his case, call witnesses in order to rebut number of elements supporting an offence? For example, in the Slobodan Milosevic case, the Trial Chamber entered a series of acquittals of the Bosnia-Herzegovina part of the case, noting that on the one hand there was no evidence adduced for some paragraphs, and on the other hand that the evidence adduced was insufficient. In a recent decision in Milutinovic et al., which was issued after the 2008 reform, the Trial Chamber in its oral decision stated, and I quote: "Where there is no evidence to sustain a count, the motion will be granted. Where there is some evidence but it is such that taken at its highest a Trial Chamber could not convict on it, the motion will also be granted. Where there is some evidence but it is such that its strength or weakness depends upon the view taken on a witness's credibility and upon one possible view of the facts a Trial Chamber could convict on it, the motion will not be granted." Similarly, the Milutinovic Chamber referred to the legal test used in the Jelisic appeals judgement and to the 98 bis decisions issued in the -- in the following cases: Slobodan Milosevic, Mrksic, Martic, and Dragomir Milosevic. The purpose of Article 98 bis is extremely clear. It is meant to prevent a trial from continuing in cases where Prosecution did not sufficiently provide proof of its allegations and in the absence of any analysis of the position of the Defence through its evidence either mentioned already adduced or to be adduced. Furthermore, since this is a very long case, we know that the accused has been in provisional custody for more than eight years. I believe, therefore, the test -- the standard of review for the evidence in Article 98 bis should be higher than in ordinary cases where there is an expeditiousness, according to the Statute of the Tribunal. It would be unfair to continue a trial when the evidence adduced so far insufficient. Note -- especially since the provisional detention has been extremely long and that -- and that Prosecution has had all its time to put the finishing touches to its investigation. Since we know that here at the ICTY the Prosecution during the trial can continue its investigation and can adduce whenever it wishes to do so new evidence, sometimes at the very last minute, as was the case with the diaries of General Mladic. I will now turn to the crimes alleged in the indictment, crimes committed in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia. As far as the crimes alleged in the indictment are concerned, I believe that some of them have been established through the evidence adduced by the Prosecution and -- but some others have not been established. In the annex that we will soon have on the screen, you will see the evidence which according to me could allow any reasonable trier of fact to conclude that there was a crime as the Statute of the Tribunal understand it. For crimes committed in municipalities, I will recall for each and every one of them what evidence has been adduced by the Prosecution in its preliminary brief as well as its oral submissions. I am not going to recall the position of the accused, because it has been given in detail when reading the majority decision of the Trial Chamber in its first chapter, review of the procedure. However, I must remind you of the position of the Prosecution in a detailed way by quoting all witnesses and documents supporting its allegations regarding the crimes, which is what I'm going to do for crimes committed in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia. Given there are a lot of references, I will be ask to be placed on the screen a summary chart of all the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. Before this, however, there are other elements I must deal with. The careful review of the elements -- of the evidence adduced and the testimonies heard by the Trial Chamber during the Prosecution case could lead a reasonable Judge to conclude that beyond any -- all doubt that the crimes alleged in the indictment were actually committed, this undisputedly except for some points which I will detail later on. It is thus possible to conclude that within the time period of the indictment, from August 1991 to September 1993, military actions were carried out in a number of towns of former Yugoslavia, notably in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Serbia, mainly in the cities of Zvornik, Vukovar, Mostar, Nevesinje, and Bijeljina, in the framework of which civilians or enemy fighters were captured. Some were detained, others were mistreated, and a large number of them were executed. The list of the victims mentioned illustrates these crimes can be found in appendix 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, and 11 of the indictment. This being said, regarding counts 12 and 13, wanton destruction of private or public property, does the Prosecution give enough evidence to prove that the crimes committed during the period mentioned in paragraph 34 of the indictment and in the cities mentioned in the indictments were actually carried out by groups on the terrain and which came under the authority either of the JNA or of the VRS? Military authority. Therefore, regarding the destruction of buildings, it is true that some of them were damaged or totally destroyed, but the report of the Prosecution expert, Mr. Andras Riedlmayer, is not such that it could -- that this destruction could be directly attributed to a single group and does not allow also to provide exact dates for this destruction. It seems that the expert used documents drafted after the events and on photographs taken before, during, or after the events. Therefore, how is it possible to say that in a given locality and in a given city a mosque which has been completely destroyed is a parking lot now, but the mosque might have been destroyed by the municipality after the events for different reasons, maybe just because this mosque was about to crumble. The expert did not answer these kinds of concerns, and I do have elements in evidence that allow me to conclude that these buildings were actually either damaged or destroyed, but I don't have enough evidence to attribute this damage, destruction, to a specific group which would have acted under the direct authority of the accused as alleged in paragraph 34 of the indictment under any modes of liability, including JCE III. I would also like to add that as far as Mostar is concerned, the many -- all these buildings might have been destroyed during the conflict between the Serbs and the Muslims and the Croats or also during the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, which introduces another element of doubt. Regarding the counts 12 and 13 dealing with the wanton destruction of private and public property, as things stand now, the following religious buildings must be excluded: In Mostar, the Nesuh Aga Vucjakovic mosque, the Franciscan monastery and the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus. In Nevesinje, the Islamic clock tower, the Hadzi Dervis Cucak mosque, the market mosque, and the Sinan Dede Efendi mosque. Regarding the municipality of Zvornik, the Mekted, and the Gusteri mosque, the new Donji Krizevici mosque, the Svrake mosque, and the Vitinica mosque. In the area of Sarajevo, the Hadzi Idriz mosque in Hrasno, and the Catholic Church of the Holy Trinity in Novo Sarajevo. Because the only buildings that should be taken into account are those who have been extremely damaged. You will see later on in the chart they will be noted LDE; or the buildings that have been partially destroyed, marked with PD; or the buildings that have been totally destroyed, CD. However, contrary to the crimes of plunder which I will expound on later, even as things stand now, there are some failings as described above. The Trial Chamber, when it deliberates, will have the -- the expert report as well as other documents, which may lead it to conclude in a very specific fashion that such-and-such building has been destroyed and this at a specific date with a specific identification of the perpetrators, and thus a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that as things stand, these destructions did occur. Regarding count 14, plunder. At paragraph 34 of the indictment, the Prosecution says that public and private properties were plundered in the municipalities of Zvornik, in Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, and Nevesinje. I believe it is necessary regarding this plunder to have at least a few intangible evidence such as the list of the victims of this plunder, an accurate description of the goods plundered, the photographs or reports on these goods, and the elements helping to identify the perpetrators, but I must note that, unfortunately, this evidence does not exist as things stand. Therefore, I cannot conclude that hundreds of houses were plundered in Vukovar, Zvornik, and the Greater Sarajevo region, in Vogosca, in Mostar and in Nevesinje. Consequently, I'm now going to show on the screen the charts which include the evidence which according to me could lead a reasonable Judge to conclude that the alleged crimes were actually committed. I will ask the court officer to place the summary chart of the evidence on -- under the ELMO. Here you have a list of all municipalities on the left-hand column. Exhibits, you have the list of the documents which according to the Prosecution are evidence of the crime. And on the other column, witnesses. You have the number of all the witnesses who testified about these crimes. This is a summary chart giving you the position of the Prosecution. I will now get into the details, and I will ask the usher to show us Annex 1, which deals with Vukovar. In this appendix, on the left-hand side you have the paragraphs in the indictment; second column is paragraphs in the pre-trial brief; footnotes in the pre-trial brief which refer, of course, to these paragraphs; and on the right-hand side column, list of the witnesses and documents which according to me can prove that crimes were actually committed in Vukovar. Paragraph 16, for example, Witness VS-011 and VS-015. I will later hand to Mr. Marcussen and Mr. Seselj these charts. Therefore, they can take a look at them. Believe me, this took hours to put together. Appendix number 2, Vocin. Same principle. You have paragraphs in the indictment, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, footnotes, and witnesses and documents supporting the allegations of the Prosecution. Then Annex 3, Bijeljina. I'm not going to go through it -- through all of these annexes, otherwise we'd be spending weeks here. So for Bijeljina you have the paragraphs in the indictment mentioning Bijeljina, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, footnotes, and witnesses and documents. Then Brcko. Same thing for Brcko, paragraph in the indictment, pre-trial brief, footnotes, witnesses and documents. For Brcko you can see that this is not supported by many witnesses, only mainly by Witness VS-1033. Annex 5, Bosanski Samac. Here again, same columns, paragraphs in the indictment, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, footnotes in the pre-trial brief, witnesses and documents. And you can note here again we have an interview of Mr. Seselj mentioned to support paragraph 16 of the indictment, paragraph 86 in the pre-trial brief. Zvornik, Annex 6. Here again for Zvornik there are two pages because it's quite extensive. Paragraphs in the indictment on the left-hand side, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief from 91 to 94. You have all the footnotes and all the witnesses who testified for Zvornik with their number and so far -- and so forth and so on. All this is at your disposal, and you can take a look at it and scrutinise it. It will probably take you hours to peruse through it. Annex 7, Greater Sarajevo. Sarajevo region. Paragraphs in the indictment, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, footnotes, witnesses and documents. And this page is the second page for Sarajevo. Then Mostar, Annex 8. One page was enough, was sufficient. In the pre-trial brief paragraphs 109 to 116, footnotes, and you have the list of all witnesses who came to talk about Mostar. You have all the necessary reference here. Annex 9, Nevesinje. There again, this tedious work -- work made it possible to illustrate all paragraphs in the indictment and the pre-trial brief, to see what footnotes and witnesses and documents correspond. And I refer to document P31, which is the testimony of Mr. Seselj under oath in the Milosevic case. And you have the transcript references, of course, in the Milosevic case, the French Milosevic case -- the French transcript, which I read extensively. Appendix 10, Hrtkovci. This is a very important city. We have the paragraphs in the indictment, paragraphs in the pre-trial brief, 122 to 129 because there's an additional page. Thank you. The witnesses who came to testify. As you see, there is -- there are many of them, and you have their numbers. I will now move on to Appendix 11. And I would like to thank our usher, who is very effective and helps us to save time. Let me explain something to Mr. Marcussen and Mr. Seselj. This chart gives a list of all Croat victims who according to the Prosecution were deported or forced to leave the area, to leave either to Croatia or elsewhere. There are several hundreds of these people. There's 28 pages of this annex. On the left -- right-hand side, I deduct all mentions of people whose destination is unknown. For example, number 4, 18, 19, and 21. Page 2, 26, 27, 28, 33, 34, 36, 40, 43, 47, and 48. For some of these people we know for sure that they did go to Croatia and Zagreb, but for others in the document, all that is stated is destination unknown. We don't know. We don't know whether they left. We don't know whether they left because they were expelled or because of forcible transfer, whether they left of their own volition. There's a doubt. Because of this I delete from Appendix 11, 233 people, which means that should Mr. Seselj be found guilty, as far as I'm concerned he should be acquitted at least for the victims who are listed on the right-hand side column, because I have no element at hand to know whether these people actually left Hrtkovci or not. We don't know where they went. And Appendix 12, which was what I had regarding the mosques and the Catholic churches. You will see there's a key. SD severely damaged, PD partially destroyed, CD completely destroyed, and AB adjacent building. Each letter gives us a qualification. I divided the religious property into two categories, Muslim sites and Catholic sites. I made a list of all the property that was severely damaged, first column; partially destroyed, second column; or completely destroyed, third column. For example, you see that the convent of Franciscan sisters was severely damaged, but the church of St. Peter and St. Paul, 19th century, was partially destroyed. This is Annex -- this is for Mostar on this page. On the next page, we have Nevesinje. Here for Nevesinje, as far as partially -- totally destroyed, completely destroyed, you have them here. And, for example, see that the Islamic archives were completely destroyed. That's on the right-hand column. Then Zvornik. This is very tedious work was done, you know, building by building, and you have the conclusions I drew regarding the -- either the total or partial destruction of these sites. For example, you see that the 18th century mosque of Begsuja was totally destroyed in Zvornik, completely destroyed. And the list goes on. Obviously, there was a huge amount of religious buildings in this city. We'll now move to the Sarajevo region. Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo. You have a list of buildings here. Vogosca. There again the buildings are divided according to the destruction they incurred. On this page you have Vogosca and Ilijas. The list for Ilijas continues on the next page. Next chart -- no, we've seen everything. We have here on this -- these charts all the evidence that could establish the commission of crimes. The next question now is who these crimes should be attributed to. In order to do so, I must mention paragraph 4, individual criminal responsibility. Modes of responsibility. In paragraph 130 of the pre-trial brief, the Prosecution asserts that individual criminal responsibility of Vojislav Seselj is incurred in the counts of the indictment pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute. That quotes paragraphs 5 to 14 of the indictment. As far as commits is concerned, Vojislav Seselj is prosecuted for having participated in the JCE and also for having physically committed (a) crimes of prosecution -- of persecution through hate speeches as part of the incidents that occurred in Vukovar, Croatia, and Zvornik, BiH and Hrtkovci, Vojvodina, Serbia, and (b) the crimes of expulsion and forcible transfer as part of the incidents that took place in Hrtkovci. As far as direct responsibility of the accused is concerned, I must address the forms of responsibility of the accused. These forms each in turn according to the following outline: Planning, instigating, ordering, committing as part of the JCE, individual commission of crimes of persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer, and aiding and abetting. I shall, after I have delivered my reasoning, enter a judgement of acquittal on several counts of the indictment. Planning. The Prosecution, in paragraph 143 of the pre-trial brief avers that the accused planned the crimes of persecution, murder, torture, cruel treatment, deportation, forcible transfer, wanton destruction, and plunder of private and public property in Vukovar and Zvornik, counts 1, 4, 8, 9, and 10 to 14. Paragraphs 15 to 18, 20 to 22, 24 to 26, 26 to 34 of the indictment. And the crimes of persecution, deportation and forcible transfer at Hrtkovci, counts 1, 10 and 11, paragraphs 15 to 17, 31 to 33 of the indictment. The Prosecution submits that the mens rea element involved in the planning of the crimes in Vukovar and Zvornik results from (a) his inflammatory speeches, (2) the fact that he approved the sending of his volunteers in these areas when he knew that they had committed criminal acts on the battle-fields. Third point: From the fact that these crimes did in fact take place, were committed. The Prosecution adds that as far as Hrtkovci is concerned, the mens rea involved in planning is exemplified by the statements made by witnesses VS-014, VS-026, VS-1133. I hold first of all that planning implies at its lowest a plan and an architect of that plan, all the more so that in Vukovar the intervention of the JNA could only take place after a decision at a very high level had been taking -- taken involving the military command and that in this context the political opponent in the person of the accused played no part in the planning. The fact that volunteers were present in Vukovar or sent to Zvornik is not, per se, enough to state that he planned or that he was involved in the planning or that he was a perpetrator in the planning. As far as Hrtkovci is concerned, the accused did not plan the deportations or the persecution campaign himself. It is important to note that at the time he delivers his speech, and for those people who have forgotten about it, this was on the 6th May -- 6th of May, 1992. He was on a campaign trail and had no means of coercing the civilian population in his capacity as a possible main perpetrator of the planning. The mens rea element involved in planning cannot be directly drawn from the inflammatory speeches, for a sufficient nexus cannot be drawn between words uttered in Vukovar, which is far from having been established, and a meeting in Mali Zvornik which did not take place at the date specified by the Prosecution, in my view. I hold, secondly, that the fact that the accused approved of the sending of -- of volunteers does not mean that he knew that some of them were going to commit crimes on the ground. In this respect, it is important to make a distinction at the moment in time when the volunteers were sent spontaneously, Borovo Selo, and the sending of volunteers at the request of Slobodan Milosevic in a legal fashion. Furthermore, as things stand, sufficient -- there is insufficient evidence to prove that a member of an SRS -- a volunteer member of the SRS committed a given crime. The fact that the alleged crimes took place does not mean that these crimes had been planned beforehand. It is alleged in the indictment and the pre-trial brief in several instances that volunteers of the SS -- of the SRS, Seselj's men, did participate in the commission of multiple crimes. If it's true that several witnesses, either in the statements they gave to the OTP or during their testimony before the Chamber mentioned the existence of SRS volunteers, Seselj's men, a reasonable trier of fact must nonetheless, to establish what one or more person has said, have material and indisputable evidence. First piece of evidence which should be indisputable, the military booklet of the volunteer, which mentions his assignment to a given post and to a military unit, identified with the initials VP and follows by a number. Refer to Goran Stoparic's witness testimony on the 15th of January, 2008, at the hearing held in open session where he explained all of this to us. The second mens rea element which should be -- which should be cross-referenced with the first element is the membership card of the SRS which each party member had.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The second material element, interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without such cross-referencing of these two elements a reasonable trier of fact cannot conclude that a given volunteer, assigned to a given unit, having committed a given crime, was a volunteer of the SRS. Furthermore, the numerous testimonies of Prosecution witnesses, photos and videos adduced and admitted by the Trial Chamber lead to the conclusion that any fighter was wearing patchy clothing and this does not mean that this qualified him as a member of a particular unit in the absence of any insignia or distinctive sign identifying the unit. Likewise, some of them wore the sajkaca, others did not, or wore a helmet or had no helmet and no sajkaca. It is clear that in light of the evidence that has been admitted, each volunteer was submitted to a military chain of command which was not in my view the chain of command of the SRS. I hold, therefore, that the accused should be acquitted on this mode of responsibility based on planning. I'm just looking at the clock. We have approximately ten minutes left. I believe that in ten minutes' time, I will have time to read three pages. I will then have completed one-third of what needs to be done. Instigation. The Chamber in its majority has decided to only look into this mode of responsibility. I myself review all modes of responsibility. The Prosecution, in paragraphs 146, 147, and 148 of the pre-trial brief ascertains by relying on various judgements and appeals judgements Kvocka, Kordic, Blaskic, Krstic, Nahimana, Brdjanin, Akayesu, that the accused instigated the crimes of persecution, murder, torture, cruel treatment, deportation, forcible transfer, wanton destruction, and plunder of private and public property in Vukovar and Zvornik, counts 1, 4, 8, 9, and 10, 10 to 14, paragraphs 15 to 18, 20 to 22, 24 to 26, 26 to 34 of the indictment. And the crimes of persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer in Hrtkovci, counts 1, 10 and 11, paragraphs 15 to 17, and 31 to 33 of the indictment. Through inflammatory speeches he delivered when he visited these localities or other neighbouring localities like Mali Zvornik. As far as was uttered by the accused in Vukovar is concerned, it so happens that the evidence adduced does not prove that the accused uttered these words. In fact, Witness VS-027. On reviewing his testimony -- or when I reviewed his testimony, realised that he is not entirely credible. All the more so that in the Mrksic, Radic, and Sljvancanin judgement that amounts to res judicata, it is mentioned in paragraph 51 the following, I shall read it out. It seems a point of interest. "The Trial Chamber reserves the right to address this in greater detail in its judgement. The Chamber is not persuaded of the honesty or reliability of the witnesses who testified about this. The evidence in this respect is not confirmed by other evidence and in addition there is contradicting evidence regarding Miroslav Radic, Veselin Sljvancanin's presence at this meeting. The Chamber recalls at this stage that it accepts that Vojislav Seselj visited Vukovar on several occasions in late October and early November 1991, but is unable to conclude on the evidence it has heard that Radic and Sljvancanin attended a meeting at which Seselj made such a statement." There is an element of doubt in my view, and this benefits the accused, of course. As far as the speech delivered at Mali Zvornik is concerned, alleged in paragraphs 93 of the pre-trial brief, addressed by the sole witness, VS-017. Quoted in a footnote on page 292, the witness seems uncertain about the date. The confusion may arise from the fact that another speech was delivered in August of 1990. As far as the speech delivered at Hrtkovci on the 6th May, 1992, is concerned, mentioned in paragraph 127 of the pre-trial brief, the statements of Witness VS-1133, quoted in the form of a footnote on page 441 do not seem credible, all the more so that the speech that the Chamber has received does not mention his statement in any way. Let me remind you of the words purportedly uttered by the -- the accused that mixed marriages needed to be purged, mixed marriages between Serbs and Croats, and that the children of this union should be killed. VS-133, line 10624 and 10664. These statements do not figure in the official speeches we have received. However, the speech delivered at Hrtkovci through the words spoken fall within the scope of counts 1, 10, and 11 of the indictment under instigation to commit persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer. At this stage of the trial, it cannot be determined whether under counts 1, 10 and 11 of the indictment the accused Seselj incited or instigated or committed, for either he instigated or he committed. He can't, in my view, be both an instigator and a perpetrator. It's either one or the other. Therefore, irrespective of this issue, the Prosecution has adduced enough evidence on the instigation of crimes of persecution, deportation, and forcible transfer at Hrtkovci. However, he should be acquitted on the crimes of murder, torture, cruel treatment, wanton destruction and plunder. That said, the documents quoted by the majority, P1264, P1259, P1257, P1192, P1293, P0685, P526, P528, P1298, P1200, P1180, P1324, and the witness testimonies of VS-016, VS-033, Stojanovic, Bosanac, and VS-004 seem insufficient to establish a nexus between the instigating statements the accused is charged with and the crimes listed under counts 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, and 14 of the indictment. I will finish in a few minutes' time. I should also mention in greater detail, counts 8 and 9 on torture and cruel treatment. The majority of the Bench relies on VS-1032 to establish the commission of the crimes in Zvornik. If it is true that the head of the unit, Cele, mistreated and killed detainees and that he was a volunteer that had been proclaimed Vojvoda, and that other volunteers headed by a so-called Repic had committed torture and cruel treatment in the municipality of Zvornik, this does not mean that a reasonable trier of fact can draw the conclusion that these acts were committed on the instigation of the Accused Seselj. Indisputable or compelling evidence, such as documents or statements, establishing a positive nexus between the crimes and the accused is required. The Chamber in its majority found that sufficient evidence was adduced with regards to count 8 and 9, instigation in Vukovar; Berghofer, VS-1051, Vojnovic, VS-016. Zvornik; VS-1012, VS-1013, VS-1064, VS-1065, P307, P389, P469. Sarajevo; VS-1055, P455, P457. Nevesinje; VS-1022, VS-1051. Mostar; Karisik, Bilic. If a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that torture and cruel treatment were, in fact, committed, there is nonetheless not sufficient evidence to establish a -- to establish a nexus between the Accused Seselj and these crimes for instigation and this form of responsibility. As an example, what words uttered led in the mind of the perpetrator of the crime to brutal and inhuman living conditions for civilians in the basement of the Kilavci thermal plant? Witness VS-1022 ascertains that this occurred, that no one doubts, but what are the reasons for that, the words uttered by the accused or any other reason? There again, I entertain doubt as to counts 7, 8, and 9, instigating to commit murder. Tomorrow, I'll look into ordering, and I will at great length develop another topic. Forgive me for that, but it is essential. I will address the issue of the joint criminal enterprise, and I may as well tell you straight ahead beforehand, because this may give you food for thought overnight. I find that Mr. Seselj was not a participant in a joint criminal enterprise together with Milosevic, Karadzic, et al. But all this will be proven and demonstrated tomorrow, based on a very lengthy reasoning that is going to be quite time-consuming tomorrow. So there it is. I got to page 25. We've got 50 pages for tomorrow. Rest assured, we won't have to work until midnight tomorrow. This being said, I wish you all a very good evening. We shall reconvene tomorrow to go on with the reading.
